An outstanding air tower, with stellar performance and a super-easy install process, complete with its own display. The only downsides? Intel support is extra, and it's strictly a "bring your own thermal paste" event.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

Where do I even begin with this thing? I'm so conflicted on the SK700V. It's such a unique problem, simultaneously excellent, and yet surprisingly frustrating to talk about. I'll start with the positive. It's exceptional. For the price, the display, the cooling, the installation process, it's next level, and I've never seen anything like it. It's honestly impressive. Without a doubt, the best air cooler I've tested in years.

But, even with that glowing accolade there, boy does it irritate me.

Let's talk features first, though, before I start to wail on the minor inconveniences that have upset my tech media brain, because the SK700V has one pretty nifty detail straddling its heatpipes, and that's namely, a full-fat display gracefully sitting atop that shiny tower.

Yep, it's a screen we've finally got them folks, air towers with screens on them. And if Computex is anything to go by this year, we're going to be seeing a lot more screens on things. Graphics cards, CPU towers, heck, I'd be surprised if we don't see them on DRAM soon. That'll bring the price down, I'm sure of it.

✅ You want an affordable, compatible CPU tower with a display: Compatible with practically all RAM kits imaginable, with exceptional performance, and a display as standard, all for sub $100. Nice.

✅ You're running hotter chips: It's solid, but don't expect it to cool your overclocked Core i9 14900K, or AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D. If that's the case you'll still want a beefy AIO behind them.

AM5, AM4, (LGA1851, LGA1700, LGA1200, LGA115X, with mounting kit)

It's not your full-fat OLED display, or anything fancy, but rather a simple digital-clock style system that actively reports on CPU frequency, temp, load, and power draw all on the fly. There's not much in the way of customisation in the software, but to be honest, there doesn't really need to be.

Sudokoo's generally quite an interesting company too. It's relatively new, founded in 2024, and is working in collaboration with a Taiwanese OEM with designs that remind me a lot of DeepCool's.

The SK700V is remarkably affordable for a licensed design. Sudokoo's pitching the SK700V at around $90 in the US and £80 in the UK, which is remarkably affordable given what you're getting here.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

I'm going to cover the irritating bits now, actually, because I want to get them out of the way, as genuinely there's a lot of good to talk about here.

Unboxing the SK700V is a real experience. The packaging is lush, pink and yellow. You open it up, and inside, in my case, there are two kits, an included Intel mounting bracket kit (which, annoyingly, Sudokoo sell separately), and a severe lack of thermal paste (although bizarrely, you do get some grease cleaner).

I don't understand why these two things are not included by default. I know that's a weird hill to die on, but there's literally zero reason why they shouldn't be included. This isn't some specially designed Noctua NH-L9i where the mounting is built directly into the low-profile frame.

This is a standard run-of-the-mill air-tower (albeit a very slim one), so why that Intel bracket isn't included is beyond me. Intel isn't dead, come on, guys. Oh, and the thermal paste too. Please, we're talking cents here, pennies, sweet naff all, include a tiny tube.

Installing it, though, was perhaps the most seamless experience I've ever had. Get your brackets set up, then take your tower, and slide the fan up and out of its rails (yes, rails). Underneath, you'll see some contact points for the display, and a hole for the included long screw driver on the back side. The front screw mount is easily reachable by any standard model. Then, once you're mounted, just slide the fan back in, clicking it into place, plug in the cables, and you're good to go. No funky, annoying metal clips, no awkward mounts, it's just brilliant. It's also remarkably compact; even with the fan in place, I could easily install memory after, no problem.

✅ You want an affordable, compatible CPU tower with a display: Compatible with practically all RAM kits imaginable, with exceptional performance, and a display as standard, all for sub $100. Nice.

❌ You're running hotter chips: It's solid, but don't expect it to cool your overclocked Core i9 14900K, or AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D. If that's the case you'll still want a beefy AIO behind them.

The software, though, was a challenge on my machine. For whatever reason, Chrome, Brave, and Edge all flagged it as untrusted, and no matter what I tried with Windows, I could not for the life of me get it to download (this is less a problem with Sudokoo, more Microsoft, being, eh, well, Microsoft). In the end, I had to download it on a Linux machine, chuck it on a USB and bring it across that way. The software's fairly barebones, but it gives you all the system stats you need, and hooks up nicely with the SK700V as well.

As for performance. Stellar. Genuinely Stellar. I tested this at an ambient temp of around 26 to 27 degrees C, and it beat almost every other single tower cooler in our testing stack. In Baldur's Gate 3, it beat almost every air tower it went up against, bar Thermalright's Peerless Assassin 120 SE, but demolished everything in Metro Exodus, was pretty good in X264, beaten only by the Thermalright and the Arctic Freezer 36, not really winning any accolades, but monstered everything in Cinebench R23. A true testament to the design, given it was operating in ambient conditions four to five degrees higher than elsewhere.

The SK700V is, for a first attempt (and I know, yes, it's technically a licensed design), remarkable. At this price point, delivering this kind of performance, it's just brilliant to see. Particularly when the rest of the industry is on such a price hike at the moment, is it perfect? No. But if you're after an affordable air tower that looks good, and delivers while it does it, well, there are few I'd recommend more.

3. Best dual-towerThermalright Peerless Assassin 120 SE

An outstanding air tower, with stellar performance and a super-easy install process, complete with its own display. The only downsides? Intel support is extra, and it's strictly a "bring your own thermal paste" event.

Since then, he’s dabbled in PR, working for Corsair for a while as its UK PR specialist, before returning to the fold as a tech journalist once again.

He now operates as a freelance tech editor, writing for all manner of publications, including PC Gamer, Maximum PC, Techradar, Gamesradar, PCGamesN, and Trusted Reviews as well. If there’s something happening in the tech industry it’s highly likely Zak has a strong opinion on it.

#4094. 'We Will Put In Our Best Efforts To Develop For It' - Stellar Blade CTO Wants Xbox Helix Dev Kit

"Personally, I am looking forward to the next-gen Xbox"

Shift Up CTO DongKi Lee, best known for his work on Stellar Blade and the studio's mobile games, recently spoke at a developer panel about his excitement to get hands-on with Xbox Project Helix development kits. All whilst in front of a senior official of team Xbox.

As Inven Global puts it, Lee was one of five panellists, comprised of execs from other development studios, and answered questions on what it's like developing games for console in the Korean gaming industry.

When asked about what advantages the console platforms have compared to PC, fellow panellist and former Tekken CEO Katsuhiro Harada took the opportunity to throw some shade at the Xbox Series S, jesting "I wish hardware like the 'Xbox Series S' wouldn't be released", attributing additional development resources to optimising games for the lower spec console.

In response to this, the Shift Up CTO spoke about his excitement to work alongside Xbox and his eagerness to see Project Helix developer kits in Korea:

"Personally, I am looking forward to the next-gen Xbox 'Helix'. From an engineer's standpoint, if you provide us with a dev kit first in Korea as early as possible, we will put in our best efforts to develop for it."

Xbox players have been asking for a Stellar Blade port for quite some time, regularly mocking up fake Xbox Series box art and posting it to socials, and usually asking when Shift Up will bring the game to Microsoft hardware. It's certainly a possibility, and DongKi Lee's enthusiasm for working with Project Helix is encouraging. That, and this tweet from Edo, Shift Up's 'publishing guy':

During the panel, Lee was asked about the recent Switch 2 version of Stellar Blade and the effort involved in porting the game from PS5 to NS2. The Shift Up CTO shared a chuckle with the panel moderator and CEO Harada whilst discussing what could and couldn't be compromised during the port. Specifically, how reducing the polygon count on protagonist Eve's 'rear' was "never an option".

#4093. Skyblivion modders reveal a former volunteer is "threatening to sue for damages upwards of €30,000" over work on the unofficial Oblivion remake project

"I just hope that we can get this resolved as soon as possible and get on with the planned release"

The team behind Oblivion remake mod Skyblivion are being threatened with legal action by a former volunteer on the project, according a video posted by current lead Kyle 'Rebelzize' Rebel. The situation looks like it'll need resolving before the mod, which was originally set to release last year, can finally make its way out of the Imperial City sewers.

"Recently, a former volunteer who contributed to Skyblivion’s development departed the project," the Skyblivion team outlined in a written statement and a YouTube video presented by Rebel. "We want to be completely transparent with the community about what has happened since their departure. After they left the project, we had several discussions regarding the continued use and maintenance of his work. The main disagreement centered on their objection to our decompilation of parts of their work — a necessary step our team took to maintain functionality and fix issues in systems already built into the project after access to the original source code repository was revoked."

"To protect ourselves from more stress and try and ensure a clean break, we decided to take the high road," Rebel explained in the video. "We have removed that work entirely. Thankfully due to some of our volunteers stepping up and simply learning new skill sets, as well as help from prominent Skyrim modders and permissions to use and integrate existing Skyrim mods, we've been able to implement replacements that we think fit Skyblivion's needs, in some cases even better than what we had before."

However, Rebel and co claim that despite them making it "clear multiple times to this former volunteer that we have removed their contributions", the ex-Skyblivion dev is "threatening to sue for damages upwards of €30,000". They claim that the ex-volunteer's legal threats "demand personal information of multiple volunteers [on Skyblivion] including full names and addresses". Rebel noted that the team see these demands as "something that we are simply not willing to share with someone that we don't even know" and feel are "just completely disproportionate for what's really going on".

The modders say they've consulted with legal counsel already and have a lawyer on standby if necessary. Though, since said lawyer's services will - the Skyblivion team claim - cost €2,500, they've put out a call for anyone with "a background in IP law or GDPR law" willing to offer them pro bono legal aid to get in touch via the mod's website.

"Please don't turn this into any kind of witch hunt, despite this very unfortunate situation," Rebel said in closing. "We don't wish ill on a former volunteer over all this and I just hope that we can get this resolved as soon as possible and get on with the planned release, which is really what we're working towards. You will hear more from us soon on the actual release."

This situation makes it two years running that Skyblivion's found itself engulfed in drama during the final months of what's supposed to be its release year. In 2025, former volunteer Dee Keyes had a public disagreement with the project's leads over whether releasing the mod that year was a reasonable or achievable goal. Skyblivion was subsequently delayed into 2026.

This past weekend, Keyes tweeted a response to the Skyblivion team's statement on the alleged legal threats. "I've had my issues with the project and left because of it, but I left knowing that my work would remain with [Skyblivion] (happily so) and didn't want to hurt the project's progress," he wrote. "I understand [the former volunteer] being upset, but I really don't see why they'd go so far as to demand their work ripped out."

Here's hoping the Skyblivion team and the ex-volunteer can resolve things without all the expense and effort that'd inevitably be necessary if the dispute ends up in court. Given there are now less than two months left of 2026, and Skyblivion's modders have this on their plates on top of any remaining work needed to finish their creation, I'd personally be very surprised if its release doesn't end up being pushed into next year.

#4091. Delve into "a deep underground facility full of secrets and horrors" in the latest Fallout 4 quest mod from the Commonwealth Story Expansion Project

A mysterious bunker with out of this world contents

After adding a whole new town to Fallout 4 last month, a group of modders have released another in their long string of extra quests for the RPG. This latest mission revolves around a dungeon delve in the Glowing Sea, where a mysterious bunker's just been unearthed.

"The harsh radioactive winds of the Glowing Sea have uncovered a deep underground facility full of secrets and horrors," the group behind the Commonwealth Story Expansion Project (CSEP) declared the description of this latest work, Under The Stars.

A fresh dungeon with a quest attached, the mod tasks you with donning your hazmat suit for a trip to a sunken bunker in the region of post-apocalyptic Boston with the least chill weather. Inside await voiced holotapes and puzzles offering clues as to what went down in this cosy corner of the Commonwealth, plus some new gear to make braving whatever lurks within worth it.

Spoilers: Judging by the screenshots, it looks like the place is an Area 51-esque hidey-hole for evidence of aliens and other cryptic oddities.

If you're unfamiliar, the CSEP lot are responsible for a bunch of popular Fallout 4 quest mods based around the likes of deadly cults, underground wars, post-apocalyptic detective work, and Brotherhood of Steel drama. While Under The Stars doesn't look have been as big an undertaking as those, that previous form points to it being an expertly-crafted addition that'll slot seamlessly into the game.

The modders have put Under The Stars together as part of a community-hosted modding jam called Fallout Flood, with this latest one based around the theme of being underground. Among the other works to have come out of it thus far are another Fallout 4 quest mod dubbed Stranded - The Oasis, a dungeon full of funky rats called the S'Laven, and a new robot enemy you can wear as a hat. It's also produced a New Vegas quest mod about exploring an abandoned NCR railway, so seems to have been very productive gathering of modding minds.

To give Under The Stars a go, your copy of Fallout 4 will need to have the Automatron and Vault-Tec Workshop DLCs.

#4089. Two Major Developers Explain Why They Like And Dislike Making Games For Xbox Series S

"I wish hardware like the 'Xbox Series S' wouldn't be released (laughs)"

Over the years, we've heard all kinds of stories from all kinds of developers about whether they either like or dislike making games for the Xbox Series S, and former Tekken boss Katsuhiro Harada falls into the "dislike" category.

In a recent panel discussion that was transcribed by the folks at InvenGlobal, Harada noticed that a senior Xbox official was in the audience, and joked that he wanted to let them know how much he isn't a fan of the Xbox Series S.

"Since a senior Xbox official is actually in attendance here today, I wish hardware like the 'Xbox Series S' wouldn't be released (laughs)."

He then went on to explain that although the low memory is "an issue" of the Xbox Series S, the hardest part is that it's actually so similar to the Series X, but with "awkwardly lower performance". Harada also pointed out that players direct their complaints to the developers rather than Microsoft if they don't like the visuals and/or performance.

"Low memory is an issue, but the hardest part is that it's a device so similar to Series X while having awkwardly lower performance [...] Furthermore, in markets like the US, there are more Series S users than Series X users, so we can't just cut corners. Yet after launch, Series S users direct their complaints at us developers rather than Microsoft, asking "Why is texture resolution lower only on Series S?"

Finally, he also noted that developing for the Nintendo Switch 2 is actually easier in some ways because it's a "distinct device for Nintendo fans", whereas the Xbox Series S is akin to "having to do extra work for a slightly weaker child" compared to putting in your "absolute best output" for the Xbox Series X.

Despite what it might seem like, a lot of this conversation seemed to be very lighthearted and full of laughs, and when Cyberpunk 2077's Paweł Sasko stepped in to highlight the benefits of the Xbox Series S including its affordable price and the ability to better optimise for low-spec platforms, Harada admitted that he made it sound a lot more attractive.

In fact, it was so convincing that Harada jokingly worried that it might lead to a similar Project Helix alternative!

Director Paweł: "Harada speaks a lot of truth. Players don't fully understand the technical context behind why fewer characters appear on screen or why visuals are downgraded. However, intensely optimizing for lower-spec platforms definitely brings the benefit of making the game run significantly better across all platforms—including PS5, high-end PCs, and handhelds like Steam Deck and ROG Ally.

And the biggest advantage of Series S is that its affordable price makes it accessible. Not every gamer can buy expensive high-end hardware, so from a developer's perspective, even if the strict constraints are painful, there is a silver lining in expanding market penetration to deliver the game to more players."

CEO Harada: "Director Paweł packaged Series S so gracefully that the Microsoft representative in the audience keeps nodding along. I'm worried they'll feel reassured and release a successor like 'Helix S' for the next-gen Xbox as well (laughs)."

It's best not to take any of this too seriously, but it does at least highlight the differing opinions throughout the industry about whether the Xbox Series S was a good or bad idea in hindsight.

From a consumer perspective at least, we reckon it was a fantastic idea. The Xbox Series S has continually managed to deliver incredible-looking games over the past six years, and in a time where console prices are constantly on the up, the Series S at least provides a somewhat affordable current-gen hardware option - at least if you find a good deal.

#4088. Feature: What Sony Live Service PS5 Games Are Still Alive?

All the cancelled projects and those that remain

Video games are cancelled internally all the time, but never in PlayStation's personal history have those cancellations had to happen in such a public manner. The current PS5 generation has seen the platform holder try to win the live service space, and a few years later, it's having to cancel most of the projects it revealed in attempting to achieve that.

To try and get a piece of the Fortnite pie, Sony made a hard and deliberate push into the Games as a Service space at the start of the PS5 generation. It acquired Destiny 2 studio Bungie to have it help the manufacturer do so, and at the height of the initiative, PlayStation planned to launch 12 live service games in just a few years.

The latest victim is Fairgames from Haven Studio, a developer set up to create the heist co-op title. It was announced in 2023, and three and a half years later, it's now been cancelled after failing to impress in a new round of private tests.

Times have changed, and company executives are finally learning you can't set out with the intention of making the next Genshin Impact or Apex Legends; it has to happen more naturally. Sony has learnt that the hard way, with many graves dug for its failed projects.

But what's still left of the push and remains in active development at PlayStation?

I'm going to document all the live service PS5 games from Sony that have been cancelled, released, and are still set to come (for now).

Here are all the PS5 games and projects Sony publicly announced or acknowledged that have now been cancelled:

Here are all the PS5 games Sony released that are considered live service:

Here are all the live service PS5 games Sony still has in the works:

By my count, that's nine game cancellations for projects Sony either confirmed or commented on publicly, six titles that have actually released, and four more that are currently in development. The disaster that was Concord means it can basically be discounted from the released list, despite the fact it did actually come out.

Then, the list of PS5 live service games currently in development could lose another title as soon as next month.

Horizon Hunters Gathering is currently being reworked into a more traditional co-op title, but if it doesn't impress in an evaluation planned for December, then it's getting cancelled too.

News PlayStation Scaling Back Horizon Live Service PS5 Game as Sony Failures Continue

Guerrilla has until December to impress Sony execs

Despite the consistent failure in the space, with only one big win to its name in the form of Helldivers 2, Sony has stated it's going to persist with live service titles. Back in June, boss Hideaki Nishino said the game model "attracts users on a global level".

He continued: "The genre itself is relatively new, and I think many people are trying various things, so we also want to continue to take on challenges within that context."

From Sony's perspective, those live service games aren't going anywhere despite the track record and industry shifts.

While multiplayer games have an even higher fail rate than single player games (honestly investors looking for safe, steady returns should stay far away from gaming) success can be massive and long lasting so it always has been and always will be a temptation for developers and publishers.

While a portion of the internet gets wrapped up in behind the scenes stuff and boycotts and what have you most gamers focus on the games they want to play (be they multiplayer or single player, first or third party) so I don’t think Sony’s live service push has hurt it any (in no small part because MS’s purchase of Activision didn’t result in Activision becoming Bethesda).

Its worth remembering that at the end of the day Sony is a listed company, it exists solely for the benefit of it shareholders. Their willingness to invest is basically driven by revenue and profit (and growth of those). A spreadsheet somewhere tells Sony that even 2 moderate successes out of 14 attempts is worth it - and until the spreadsheet says differently they'll keep doing it. Business isn't about love and passion and joy - its simply about the spreadsheet I'm afraid.

@AdamNovice Yeah, monetisation would certainly be a problem. The first Faction had severe pay-to-win issues with its various weapons. I think it could lean a little into the ARC Raiders style of cosmetics, but you're right; it's a very grounded world, so finding a balance of appealing but also lore appropriate would be tough.

What a waste of their talents, for me that was the one that hit hardest when closed, especially when it was rumoured they were to follow Demons Souls remake with Bloodborne remake.

Luckily Jim Ryan is out. He was the one that wanted every studio to develop a free to play game. I'll say that starting next year Sony will be back to normal. We are getting Kena, Laufy (GOW), Intergalactic and I'm pretty sure there are more unannounced exclusives. Surprise hits like Phantom Blade 0. And we have FF Revelation and Tomb Raider.

I can't foresee 4Loop ever being released. I usually like third-person shooters but I played the first beta a few months ago and everything about this game was amateurish. Confusing interface, terrible muddy graphics, no real gameplay loop, awful maps, and the controls felt dreadful. Just no fun to play at all.

It's funny to think that the one with guaranteed success (TLOU online) was cancelled because they were afraid the game's success would be not good for Naughty Dog...Management at Sony....

@Carnage Live-service is not the same as multiplayer.

Genshin is a predominantly single player focused live-service. Most single player mobile games are live-service. Quake 3 Arena really isn't in any worthwhile definition of the term.

PlayStation has wasted millions on this push. Besides consumer sentiment, we can clearly see most of their projects have ended in failure. What Xbox does/did doesn't change any of that.

I'm no stranger to slapping "Reddit" on the end of a Google search about a product to see what the unwashed masses (myself included) think about it. Assuming we're not reading bot comments, it's a great way to get a feel for a product you've not tested yourself. That's traditionally involved trawling various threads yourself, but now 'Reddit Reviews' is launching, which will collect user opinions on products and use them to inform dedicated reviews for them on Reddit's site.

"Today, we are starting to test Reddit Reviews, a new experience that organizes product conversations from across Reddit into dedicated reviews and highlights the most important takeaways from across our communities. With Reddit Reviews, people can now more easily understand what a product is really like and feel confident deciding whether it’s right for them."

AI is involved, of course: "Reddit Reviews uses AI to both organize these conversations where people describe their product experiences, and to surface the nuance, context, and connection to the original conversation."

Once it rolls out to you, you'll be able to search Reddit for reviews or for categories of products, and you'll also be able to navigate to relevant categories and similar products from the review you're looking at. In each review, you'll be shown the ratio of positive, mixed, or negative conversations about the product, as well as peoples' likes and dislikes, and you'll be able to filter in/out what's most relevant to you.

There's another aspect to this, too—a monetary one: "Many reviews also include images, prices, and purchase links where supplied by brand and retailer catalogs."

Presumably that will be an affiliated link that gives Reddit some small percentage of of any money spent, though I can't say for sure. If so, this could be another crucial revenue stream for Reddit.

While Reddit Reviews is only rolling out to US iOS users over the coming weeks and will cover around 10,000 products, the company says, "Throughout 2027, we plan to add more products and categories to Reddit Reviews and expand beyond the US."

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

Speaking of the elephant in the room, though—the possibility that people could be steered to Reddit for these amalgamated reviews rather than to sites like yours truly—I'm not too concerned. People already go to Reddit to check out user opinions on products; I do the same. I don't think collecting all those opinions up will change much in that regard, only make it a bit easier to do. It's a good move, I reckon.

Though how it pans out in practice is an open question. There's a chance, for instance, that it could open the door to review bombing. If enough people hate a company, for instance, they could band together to write badly about a product and then get its 'official' amalgamated Reddit review looking negative.

I'll be interested to see how (or if) Reddit deals with such things, as well as the opposite: companies using bots to speak highly of their own products.

#4086. Fewer genAI clones of "someone else's specific game" should flood the net going forwards, as Anthropic tell Claude to stop messing with some stuff other people own

It will still let people generate "original" games using the tech

Anthropic have told their genAI tool Claude to start ducking requests from users to recreate or clone existing games, following a flood of folks using the tech to generate six-fingered remakes. Instead of risking infringing on the intellectual property of series or titles that companies which aren't Anthropic own, Claude will instead restrict itself to only generating "original" games slopped together based on whatever data it's drawing on.

"We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy," Anthropic staffer Addy Osmani wrote on not Twitter in response to a rando with a cat profile picture having spotted the change.

"Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working," Osmani continued. "We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way." Game Developer reached out to Anthropic for confirmation and were pointed to Osmani's post.

The change should make it harder to add to the horde of genAI-powered decomps, recomps, and ports which have hit the net recently. It's hardly a surprising one, given studios like Bethesda have seemingly had to take matters into their own lawyers' hands to get the likes of an AI-generated Fallout game taken offline, with games that've just been ripped wholesale or barely tweaked likely on even more perilous ground. That said, not every corp's responded to the DIY decompilation craze by immediately taking legal action.

There's a serious degree of irony to Anthropic slapping Claude and telling it stealing is bad. One of the ways the company develop and train their genAI models is by scraping publicly available data from the internet via a web crawler.

So, some nicking of stuff is bad, little bot people keep asking to regurgitate stuff into slop they can then try to pass off as something they've created. But not all nicking of stuff, lest our whole business be on rather shaky ground.

It's unlikely this move from Anthropic does much to convince actual developers of original games they're safe to put demos of their games out prior to release, without risking dickheads using genAI to clone said demo and potentially release a slop version in rapid fashion, but one can dream of that genie being put back in the bottle someday.

#4085. Fix up towering robots while battle rages outside in Bay 12: Mech Repair, a first-person job sim with some handsome heavy duty analog tech

The most important thing to know about Bay 12: Mech Repair is that these are mechs of the MechWarrior or possibly Patlabor school – that is, basically WW2 tanks on hydraulic legs, with cockpits full of switches and wireframe displays. Their bodies are assemblages of pistons and reactors. They are not biomechs like the ones in Evangelion. An Evangelion Repair game would be… different. Less industrial, more Oedipal. You would dread removing the smallest piece of housing.

Which isn't to say that Bay 12: Mech Repair represents life on Easy Street, exactly. There's a big war happening outside, its fortunes palpable in the minced leg joints and pocked torsos of the war-bots lowered into your hangar. You're also fed details about the lives of pilots when you accept a work order. Lieutenant Iona Vale of the 3rd Recon Company says there's "left leg hesitation after extended operation", especially at higher temperatures. That sure sounds like a thing that could get Lieutenant Iona Vale killed.

It's not clear whether you can diagnose faults incorrectly, and shape the progress of the conflict, but the context brings extra emotional charge to what might otherwise be a cosy process of glueing together very expensive Air-Fix models, for all the sense of scale.

Bay 12: Mech Repair follows a familiar flow, as job sims go. Banged-up Iron Giants arrive in a steady procession. You figure out what's wrong with them based on scans, pilot reports, and so forth. Then you get out there with a welder, drill and spanner to make it right. Busted parts can be salvaged for scrap for custom components. Completed work orders net you credits that must be divided between restocking your inventory and buying new tools.

You also have the option of clearing away rust and applying a new paintjob. I'm fascinated to know if this has any real impact on either the story or your fortunes, because I guarantee that I am going to spend far more time obsessing over dazzle camouflage than giving the ol' actuators a haircut.

Read more on Steam. The devs, Crimson Herring Studios, are them wot did Sovereign Syndicate, an apparently decent Victorian fantasy RPG that we never found time to review. Look, I am not made of thumbs and eyeballs. As for the daunting possibility of an Evangelion Fixing Sim, the recently announced Valkyrie Iteration gets into some of the squirming detail, there.

#4084. Xbox Brings Its Free Tier Of Cloud Gaming To Loads More Players Today

You may recall that back in July, Xbox announced a new free version of Xbox Cloud Gaming that would allow you to play games at no charge, but you'd be forced to deal with ads as a compromise.

That tier of Xbox Cloud Gaming was in testing for months, but as of today (November 11th), it's rolled out publicly - meaning the vast majority of Xbox users around the world should now have access to it.

Xbox has been very quiet about it today so far, but based on what we've seen around the web, the free tier of Xbox Cloud Gaming will provide you with a 30-minute slot to stream "select games from your library" as well as select free-to-play games, after which time you'll be kicked off and will have to start a new session.

You'll see ads before the session begins, and seemingly never again throughout your 30-minute playtime.

"You can stream select games for free by watching ads before each gaming session. Session time limits apply. After a session ends, you can watch another set of ads to start a new session."

News Xbox Introduces Free Game Streaming With Ads, Outlines Five Principles They'll Adhere To

Rolling out now as a "test" for Xbox Insiders

Despite the rapid session length, this could prove a popular option for anyone who wants to play GTA 6 on Xbox One (for example) without being forced to pay anything for Xbox Cloud Gaming. We'd urge some caution for now though, as Xbox has yet to confirm whether GTA 6 will be one of the "select" games that supports this feature.

Meanwhile, the cloud playtime limits that were announced a while ago for Xbox Game Pass members have now started kicking in, which also means you can now purchase "Cloud Playtime" to top it up if you run out.

The prices for this here in the UK are as follows:

Curiously though, I've checked the new "Cloud Playtime" option in the Settings menu on my Xbox Series X and I'm being informed that I've still got "Unlimited" access to Xbox Cloud Gaming with my Ultimate membership, so it might be worth checking the same thing on your end and seeing what it says for you.

I'm not the only person who's spotted something similar:

Anyway, we've thrown Xbox's official tweet up above, and you can hit the link in it to find out even more details.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned "effective immediately," the company has announced following allegations of the leader having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy – and further reports of a second affair surfacing just yesterday.

In a press release shared today, Nvidia confirms that chief financial officer and executive vice president Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while the company's board searches for a permanent replacement for Huang.

Despite the circumstances, Nvidia still speaks highly of Huang in the statement. "Jensen's contributions to NVIDIA are profound," it begins. "NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry."

Huang admitted to having an affair earlier this week, but the situation was even more complicated than it could have been due to allegations that the person he was having that affair with might be a Chinese spy. Nvidia launched an investigation, with Huang acknowledging the "national security concerns" and saying he will "cooperate fully." He added: "I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American."

Beyond that, more recent reports alleged that Huang was also engaged in a second affair with one of his employees – specifically, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, Kimberly Powell. After this, it was claimed that the company's board was meeting to decide whether to oust Huang.

Nvidia's leadership change here is unprecedented – Huang has served as the company's sole CEO since its founding 33 years ago. In addition to Kress taking over in the interim, Nvidia has announced that it has appointed its first chair of the board, Harvey C. Jones, the former CEO of Synopsys.

“NVIDIA's strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," Kress says. "We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders."

Before this news, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney said that firing Huang "would be an Apple firing Steve Jobs level of idiocy."

#4082. You can make a vampire hunter who's afraid of the dark, disease and small spaces in Hunter: The Reckoning - Deathwish, and that's surely the best way to play

A month or two back I penned a 1500 word whine about feeling too powerful in Blood of Dawnwalker. "Gimme a vampire sim in which I'm a pathetic vein-nibbling goblin," I wrote, using many more adjectives than that. Well, never let it be said that I'm biased against vampires, for I am equally keen to play an RPG in which I am the least capable vampire hunter in the universe. A vampire hunter who screams when he wakes up with his hair over his face. A vampire hunter who has to spray the vampires with antibac before staking them.

An RPG like Hunter: The Reckoning – Deathwish, perhaps, which presents you with a choice of Advantages and Flaws when creating a character. You have to balance these out on a gnarly weighing scale, before they'll let you through the game's front door. Here is a video showing all that off, together with a lot of sixpacks.

The Advantage/Flaw system looks familiar on the surface. Advantages include Warrior, which gives you +15% chance of a critical hit, or Charmer, which gives you a +1 to Persuasion skill checks. Flaws include clumsy, bad reputation, fear of darkness, hypochondriac, and claustrophobia.

I don't know much about the tabletop game on which Deathwish is based, and the video skims the detail here, but I suspect the last three Flaws will boil down to something like "-1 Constitution in Unlit Closets". Still, I really enjoy the idiocy of going up against crypt-dwelling undead while being unable to tolerate shadows, small spaces, and disease. In general, I'd love it if Hunter: The Reckoning – Deathwish steered well away from any possibility of simply overpowering the vamps, to say nothing of the werewolves and other creatures of the night.

This appears to be the idea: devs Teyon have stressed their desire to make something more story and investigation-driven, after the stomping gibfest that was RoboCop: Rogue City. As narrative designer Mateusz Działowski put it in a previous dev diary, they've "switched from action with RPG elements into RPG with action elements". Amongst other things, you'll need to put together a team of fellow would-be slayers, each with secrets and traumas, and gather clues about best tactics while roaming the game's condensed and shiny New York City. You can read more about it all on Steam.

The Primals' Eikichi Iwai has died at the age of 57.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Final Fantasy 14 players have been gathering en masse across servers today in the wake of the news that Eikichi Iwai—the bassist behind the game's band The Primals—has passed away at the age of 57.

A post went out on The Lodestone in the early hours of this morning (November 11) which read: "Thank you very much for your continued support of The Primals. As announced earlier today, we are deeply saddened to share the news of the sudden passing of bassist Eikichi Iwai.

"Having witnessed his truly unforgettable performance on stage at the recent Final Fantasy 14 Fan Festival in Japan, the sudden news of his passing has come as a profound shock. The members of The Primals and the entire FF14 Development and Operations teams are overcome with deep sorrow.

"As we reflect on all that Eikichi-san has left behind, our thoughts are with him, and we offer our heartfelt condolences."

The Primals is Final Fantasy 14's in-house band, fronted by composer Masayoshi Soken and localisation lead Michael-Christopher Koji Fox, and accompanied by Tetsuya Tachibana, GUNN, and Iwai himself.

Iwai's bass in particular has elevated a ton of already-excellent tracks across the game's history: Stormblood's Amatsu Kaze, Shadowbringers' To the Edge, Endwalker's Scream and Close in the Distance, and Dawntrail's Ride the Rhythm just to name a few. The Primals has just come off the back of a strong year for live performances, too—from their usual appearance at all three Fan Festivals that took place this year, to even taking the stage at the UK's biggest rock and music festival as part of Download's lineup.

A quick trip through some of Final Fantasy 14's European servers have seen tons of players gathering in main hubs like Limsa Lominsa to pay their respects and share what it is about Iwai's work that meant so much to them. As I write this story, players and campfires line the perimeter of Omega's Limsa Lominsa plaza—a common practice for honouring the passing of key community figures and beyond, something which I've previously witnessed for the likes of Berserk's creator Kentaro Miura and Dragon Ball creator Akira Toriyama.

It's a small gesture, but one which is a pleasant reminder of why Final Fantasy 14 continues to maintain such an iron grip on myself and many others.

#4080. itch.io will soon let you filter games with genAI disclosures out of your search results on the site, after admitting it was previously "critically lacking"

itch.io has unfortunately, much like Steam, long had an issue with genAI content being uploaded in droves, drowning out perfectly good games made by human hands. The apparent standard method against this, voluntary genAI disclosure, has been itch's primary tool to combat this wave of low-quality slop, but hasn't worked out too well; itch revealed a few days ago that 'the number of game pages being created per-day has doubled in the past two months'. Now, in attempts to further combat this, beyond just game assets requiring a genAI disclosure to upload as they have for two years, itch will be expanding the mandatory disclosure to tabletop games, books, comics, and soundtracks, as well as adding a 'no AI' filter directly into the search function.

itch noted in this announcement that its previous moderation of genAI use in projects had been "critically lacking", presumably referring to the unfathomable exponential increase in games being uploaded in the past few months by people who don't give a fuck about creating anything themselves and happily contribute to the death of the planet. itch went on to post "Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop" which, I mean, sure, cool! And, look, as many, many people in itch's replies have pointed out, this is not the same as outright banning AI.

Unfortunately, my question at that point becomes: how? itch is not Steam, not a storefront backed by a gigantic corporation with support staff and quality assurance (which, you know, hasn't helped Steam much either). itch is one full-time employee with several contractors and volunteers. If there is a site-wide ban on genAI, people who use genAI will just start lying and sneaking it into their projects anyway. So, then, users just report the offenders, surely? This then requires a manual verification system, which, as is suggested by the sheer amount of games being uploaded every day, is just not feasible, let alone for a team as small as itch. And, frankly, I don't have a better solution here! This is fucked! What itch is doing is, currently, kinda the best it can right now?

itch is a beautiful thing that allows for people who just want to start making games, making art, making music, making books, to have a free space to share it with the world, and gain eyes on their work as well as necessary feedback to improve. It's less of a store and more of a forum for creators and self-published games to interact, guide one another to new, niche, cool shit. Hell, I made a visual novel and posted it on there, becoming another one of those millions of people for whom itch is a valuable platform for first creations. To have this vital space on a path to ruin as a result of the same vile tech that is also on the verge of pushing the global economy over a cliff due to its creators being caught in their multi-year lies is not a future I hope for itch. This is a step in the right direction, and one I genuinely hope pans out well for it in the long run.

#4079. "There’s always a night when Rome burns": South Of Midnight director says that Xbox funding it was "unsustainable", at least in hindsight

"I didn’t know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it"

Compulsion Games parted ways with former owners Xbox, having landed on the long list of things Microsoft were determined to ditch as part of multi-round mass cuts this year. Now, South of Midnight creative director David Sears has suggested that an eventual pulling of the rug was something he feared throughout the game's development, to the point where he seemingly doesn't think he'd have funded it if he'd been in the shoes of Xbox execs.

In an interview with MinnMax, Sears - who left Compulsion in March 2025 - outlined that ideally games big publishers put out aim to fall into one of two buckets. They either make lots of money or increase the prestige of the brand by becoming cultural touchstones across multiple generations. Obviously doing both is the perfect outcome, but Sears pegged South of Midnight as being more geared towards the latter camp. The likes of Double Fine's Keeper and Obsidian's Pentiment are other games which off the top of my head could be said to fit that same mold. The issue, of course, is that when push comes to shove, it's the games which can show a strong bottom line at any given moment which make the best case for their studios' short term survival if cash is tight.

So, South of Midnight lived in a risky place, with Sears recalling: "I literally told people. I was like, yeah, this could be terrible because somebody is going to say, one day, 'The money tap, we're closing those floodgates' and that's going to have really traumatic results downstream". The interviewer then asked Sears if what he was getting at is that, while he's glad Xbox funded South of Midnight, he might not have done so or at least cut the funding earlier if he was in charge of the console maker.

"Yeah, probably," Sears replied. "I mean, I wanted to make it. No doubt. Obviously, because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else's money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah, because I'm not completely selfless. It just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable. So, of course, it was going to have a 'shocking' outcome. I mean, it's easy to dissect it now, right? But at the time, I would talk to other directors and [they] would be like, 'How is this happening? I mean, how did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?' And I would always be like, 'For now'. There's always a night when Rome burns and I didn't know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it."

Notably, Sears added that in his view modern Microsoft showed a "more humane" side than the version of the company that existed in the 90s and early 2000s by giving studios like Compulsion a chance to spin out on their own rather than simply shuttering them outright once they were deemed surplus to requirements.

Given the director's no longer at Compulsion, it seems he'll not have a say on what their next game looks like, but as a newly indie studio one would imagine they'll have a keen eye on the bottom line.

#4078. Skyrim Celebrates 15th Anniversary with Creation Club DLC Bundle, Big Sales, and More

The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim is officially 15 years old today, having originally launched on the 11th November, 2011.

And no, Bethesda doesn't have a new re-release lined up or anything like that, so the memes will have to be put on hold for now.

But that doesn't mean the developer's forgotten about its most successful RPG. To celebrate the occasion, it's reduced Skyrim: Special Edition's price by 80% on PS5 and PS4, cutting it all the way down to $7.99 / £6.99.

Buyers can then upgrade to the Anniversary Edition, which, as far as I can tell, still costs $19.99 / £15.99. Anniversary Edition is the one that bundles all of the Creation Club stuff into the deal.

If you somehow haven't played Skyrim before, or you've just never got around to it on PS5, it's a decent discount — although it's also worth pointing out that the Special Edition is currently available through a PS Plus Extra subscription as well.

Next up, Bethesda's curated a Creations (premium mods verified by the developer) bundle for the anniversary. It throws together five of the most highly rated Creations available at a heavily discounted price.

If you were to buy all of these Creations separately, they'd set you back 3,000 credits — roughly $28 / £27, since you have to buy separate 'Creation Credits' packs.

This bundle is going for 1,500 credits, which amounts to buying 500 and 1,000 Creation Credits at $15 / £14.

Obviously Skyrim's fan-crafted DLCs aren't everyone's cup of tea, but some of them really do fall in line with what you'd expect of an official release. Legacy of Orsinium in particular is a borderline expansion, and it's got a lot of fans.

Beyond all of this, The Elder Scrolls Online is unsurprisingly getting in on the action. You can unlock Skyrim-themed rewards by taking part in the MMO's current 'Golden Pursuit' campaign.

"Fans can also expect a week full of giveaways, community spotlights, and social content," Bethesda's press release adds.

When was the last time you played Skyrim? Dare I ask if you'll be venturing back to its snowy lands for this anniversary? Shout at something in the comments section below.

Tarantino gets candid on table read issues in a new book

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Quentin Tarantino revealed he once fired one of his Inglourious Basterds lead actors after a "terrible" table read.

In an excerpt from Jay Glennie's The Making of Quentin Tarantino’s Inglourious Basterds (via People), the director said Mélanie Laurent – who played cinema owner Shosanna in the 2009 film – didn't make a good first impression.

"Mélanie Laurent’s table read was terrible," Tarantino recalled, adding, "it wasn’t good enough to be terrible."

Tarantino wrote of the experience, "A table read with the whole cast is so exciting and so important to me. Well, Mélanie was terrible, so I fired her."

Of course, that wasn't the end for the French actor. Laurent said she was ill and would wait to read again for Tarantino – who agreed to "turn the clock" back across multiple days of rehearsals.

Some on Inglourious Basterds weren't so lucky, however. Tarantino said Isabelle Huppert was replaced by Maggie Cheung for a role that was ultimately cut after missing the table read entirely.

On chopping and changing actors prior to filming, Tarantino remarked, “I have fired actors in the past. If it’s not right, it is not right. I don’t owe them shit. I owe my film the best actors I can find. Period.”

Inglourious Basterds stands as one of Tarantino's most iconic, and instantly quotable, movies. Starring Brad Pitt, Christoph Waltz, Eli Roth, and Michael Fassbender, follows an alt-history revolution against Nazi leadership in 1940s France.

Next up from Tarantino is new play The Popinjay Cavalier, starring Sacha Baron Cohen. The production is set to debut in London's West End from February 2027. The wait, then, for the director's 10th – and possibly final – film goes on.

#4075. Arc Raiders devs Embark insist that using genAI for voice lines was necessary, as "actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that"

Despite taking the voice performances of actors and feeding them into machines to spurt out AI-generated mimicry, Embark CCO Stefan Strandberg insists that "we are not in the industry of replacing actors." In a new video posted to the Arc Raiders channel focused on audio design, Strandberg refers back to the infamous use of genAI in Arc Raiders to generate voice lines based on real voice actors' performances, something which the game was heavily (and rightly) criticised for before and since its release.

In that linked piece (thanks Oisin!), CEO Patrick Söderlund stated that they have been replacing lines that were originally generated with actual recorded lines, presumably because Arc Raiders has made quite a bit of money and now they feel that they can continue paying actors to record more lines, rather than just scraping their talents and avoiding the dreaded fee of paying professionals for their work. This choice already came after their previous game, The Finals, was heavily criticised for the exact same thing, which is just a fascinating series of decisions to consider.

In the video, audio director Bence Pajor explains that the apparent reason for the use of AI was to avoid the "stress" of having to work around actors' availability, as they may be busy working on other projects when Embark decides that a new feature needs new voice lines recorded. Pings, quests, and in-level mission briefings were thus generated using training data based on existing actors' recordings, saving the need to actually get anyone back in a studio or pay them for their time. Citing the amount of variables that the ping system creates, Pajor claims it "becomes too impractical to record every possible version of something. The actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that", which is a take that falls apart if you consider the simple fact that games of this scope (or bigger) have been managing to work around actors' availability for as long as genAI has not been an accessible technology, which has been almost all of the time that video games have existed. Isn't it crazy that games like Disco Elysium and Baldur's Gate 3 had so, so much recorded dialogue, all without genAI? Or fellow live service shooter Apex Legends, which has been adding and adjusting voice lines via updates for years? How could they possibly have managed it?

Voice actresses Jo Rideout and Diana Gardner, who play Shani and Celeste respectively, are also featured speaking on their characters' relationships as well as their experience working within this hybrid model of recording and generating voices. Gardner notes that "if they only need an hour of my time for a couple call-outs that are short, then I don't have to cancel other shoots or some other project that might also be interesting. So in that way, I feel quite good about it." She then explains that "the contract seemed fair…so it was a no-brainer in that sense. But I didn't know what to expect once I heard the voice come out. I was like, 'Can I take ownership for the performance?' This is hours of work that I've put in, but can I take ownership for the final product? No."

Strandberg goes on to elaborate on his comment on not replacing actors by saying that "We are not in the industry of replacing actors, actually, I think quite the opposite. We should celebrate the performance, and we should give them more space." While Embark's audio team are indeed working on replacing the generated lines with actual performances, that doesn't change the fact that the choice to use AI in the first place was one made simply to save money in not paying actors for their specific work and get the game out the door faster — effectively the 'we'll fix it in post' of games development. While I can respect Garner's awareness that it means she can prioritise other projects when necessary, there is that notable tinge of regret in not being able to take ownership for her hours of work. Fundamentally, Embark has demonstrated its willingness to cut talent to cut costs, seemingly happy to post PR videos implying they had no choice due to the game's scope, and that isn't something a company just goes back on once they realise how 'efficient' it can be.

#4074. Workers & Resources: Soviet Republic's next DLC is set to expand the city building sim into the one place not corrupted by capitalism: SPACE

Following not the inherent liberal capitalistic framework of city builders like SimCity but instead a revolutionary (sorry) interpretation of planning and logistical simulation that prioritises centralisation and minute detail, Hooded Horse and 3DIVISION's Workers & Resources: Soviet Republic offers a tense, socialist look at what a citybuilder could be. Fellow contributor Sin Vega, in her 1.0 review, described it like this: "You have to build things to demolish things. That might be Workers & Resources in a nutshell. You're not managing budgets (money is exclusively for imports/exports), you're organising stuff." Now, having previously expanding out of the Soviet Republic and across the globe with the World Maps DLC, the next step for socialist citybuilding is, of course, space. Our Edwin outright predicted this two years ago, correctly calling that "the logical endgame here is to go to space." Good on him.

The Space Program DLC, set to release on November 23rd, will add a variety of new technologies and types of industry to the builder. It looks like it'll focus on not only the actual rockets that get into space, and the spectacle of it all, but also the huge amounts of science and industry that get to the point of rockets not exploding upon takeoff. For example, while it's all well and good for Space Program's scientists to be able to design rockets that are capable of remaining together for long enough to land safely, the designs they dream of still have to be built, meaning that industrial pipelines must be effectively centralised to ensure that every single component is of high quality and arriving in the required quantity.

The update also specifies the Sputnik and Vostok programs as elements of the expansion, implying a close historical aspect to it — though, elsewhere, "an unprecedented duel with nature" is mentioned, which is referring to either the simple harshness of space or aliens. Jury's out. A 1960s campaign will be a star feature of the DLC, which is described as a place for players to learn the new mechanics "in relative peace, surrounded by a happy, healthy, and economically stable utopia." What an idea.

There's a golden rule of storage: no matter how much you have, it's never quite enough. Nevertheless, Kioxia is taking that principle to its limits, as it's announced "a new storage density milestone" in the form of 640 of its 245.76 TB enterprise SSDs chained together to create just over 157 petabytes worth of storage in a single rack cabinet.

157 petabytes is... well, it's 157 million gigabytes. Enough storage space for God of War: Ragnarok, a 190 GB game, to be installed over 820,000 times.

And yes, it's been designed for AI data centers. The "storage solution" (I do hate that term) has been created in collaboration with Dell, and essentially amounts to 16 PowerEdge R7725xd servers, each stuffed with 40 Kioxia LC9 Series drives inside one industry-standard 42U server rack.

"As AI workloads drive continued growth in unstructured data, organizations need storage that can deliver higher capacity without a corresponding increase in data center floor/rack space, power consumption or cooling requirements," says the press gumph. "High-capacity NVMe SSDs can help address these demands by consolidating more data into a smaller, more efficient infrastructure footprint."

Which seems timely. With physical data center size becoming an increasing issue (not least because massive data center buildouts are a tad unpopular right now), cramming as much storage as possible into a single rack is sure to save on some concrete, at the very least.

But I'm not going to suggest this sort of excessive consumption is anything but jarring, given us little ol' consumers are counting our pennies in the middle of a NAND flash crisis. Have you seen the price of game-ready SSDs recently? I have. It ain't pretty.

But hey, at least we know where 157 petabytes-worth of raw flash capacity is going. Straight into one of these rack cabinets, where it can be used for all sorts of AI-related purposes. The sometimes-intelligent beast needs feeding, and Kioxia and Dell appear to have worked very hard to fit its lunch inside one handy box.

#4072. I'm sad that the Like A Dragon creator's new studio is closing, but I wish their now-cancelled debut Gang of Dragon wasn't just LAD again

Less than a year after the announcement of their first game, and only four years after the studio's creation, Gang of Dragon developers Nagoshi Studio have been dissolved by a shareholders' resolution (thanks, Gematsu.) That also means a premature end for Gang of Dragon, which was announced at last year's Game Awards with a flashy trailer featuring Like a Dragon-esque realistic visuals, combat and exploration through Kabukicho, a couple new elements like actual gunplay and car chases, as well as the star power of actor Ma Dong-seok (a.k.a. Don Lee). Following reports in March that NetEase, the studio's source of funding, would be pulling said funding in May due to ballooning costs reaching around seven billion yen, the time has sadly come for Nagoshi Studio, having not found any alternative funding sources in the time since.

Gang of Dragon looked very much to be 'just Like a Dragon again', which I find to be something of a depressing fate for a studio headed by the original series' creator. Having left Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio following Judgment and Yakuza: Like a Dragon, two of its most innovative games both with new protagonists and one entirely new turn-based gameplay style, it feels indicative of the industry that Nagoshi was granted funding seemingly on the condition that the studio makes something that just looks like the rest of the Like a Dragon series. I love Ma Dong-seok as an actor, but his presence was one of the more blatant, 'look, we got that guy!' castings of the LAD archetype, which is saying something considering Infinite Wealth had fucking Danny Trejo in a prominent role. The trailer closing with a shot of Dong-seok framed by Kabukicho's torii gate, maybe the most famous image from the Like a Dragon series, put a sour taste in my mouth as being just more of the same brand recognition (yet, for a new IP!) to prioritise safe return on investment.

I'm unfortunately not that surprised to see Gang of Dragon and Nagoshi Studio lost to time, though I am sad about it. I have some conflicted feelings on Nagoshi as a person/auteur, but I don't think he, or his studio, deserves to have funding pulled before they could even release anything as a result of NetEase deciding to pull investments out of non-Chinese companies over time. It's unknown what Nagoshi and the team will be attempting next, but I truly hope they can eventually make something. No More Heroes studio Grasshopper Manufacture was able to detach themselves from NetEase very recently and possibly avoid a similar fate, so it might not be impossible.

#4071. GTA 6 Gets 20 Seconds Of New Gameplay, And Everyone Can't Believe How Real It Looks

Here's a bit more footage that has also just appeared today:

Original Story: Sorry to keep bombarding you with GTA 6 hype, but we're literally one week away from the biggest video game launch of all time, and even 20 seconds' worth of gameplay is getting millions of views ahead of November 19th's launch.

This latest footage comes from a weird source - an Instagram account called "Only in Dade". The gameplay shows someone cruising down the road and looking at supercars out the window, while a mass of NPCs are also shown either admiring the vehicles or just making their way down the street.

Here's the footage (we can't embed the original, so you'll find the Reddit repost below):

This is clearly a marketing stunt and not necessarily representative of what you'll be seeing in the game, but it does appear to be real GTA 6 footage - Rockstar Games was spotted sharing and liking the video shortly after it went live.

It also appears to be a take on a similar real-life video from Miami that was taken last month:

Our best look at gameplay for GTA 6 to date has still been the Extended Preview from back in August, which certainly gives us a better idea of what to expect than 20 seconds' worth of gameplay.

We'll take anything we can get at this point though, and it's making the wait even harder for November 19th!

#4070. Poll: 15 Years Later, Is Skyrim Still One of the Best Open World RPGs Out There?

11/11/11 — the famous release date that will forever be associated with The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim.

If you haven't already realised, today marks the title's 15th anniversary, and it's crazy to think that the open world RPG remains one of the most consistently popular games out there.

Indeed, at the time of writing this article, Skyrim's racking up around 40,000 concurrent players on Steam. Again, it's 15 years old!

There's no denying that Skyrim has a unique magic to it; an atmosphere, a sense of time and place. Bethesda struck absolute gold with this one, despite its often obvious flaws as a role-playing excursion.

Of course, the fact that Skyrim's simply never been replaced probably bolsters its legacy. The wait for The Elder Scrolls 6 has felt eternal at points, and the long, long awaited sequel is reportedly still years away from release.

I mean, would you be at all surprised if we got a PS6 port of Skyrim before Sentinel's arrival?

But Skyrim also owes so much of its longevity to its players. Modders have kept the candle burning for over a decade, and people are still forging ahead with extremely ambitious projects today.

No game maintains that level of interest without being special in the first place, however. I'd argue that even now, there's no open world RPG quite like Skyrim — it's a truly timeless experience with regards to its gameplay loop, dynamic happenings, and player-driven sense of adventure.

I've seen Skyrim dubbed Distractions: The Game, and that comedic description still rings true. I've lost track of how many times I've started a new Skyrim playthrough over the years, but somehow, it's never lost its appeal — and that's primarily because of how freeform it can feel.

But do you think Skyrim still stands tall as an all-timer RPG? Dare I ask if you're still playing it in 2026? Vote in our polls, and then tell me all about your wintry adventures in the comments section below.

Robert (or Rob if you're lazy) is an assistant editor of Push Square, and has been a fan of PlayStation since the 90s, when Tekken 2 introduced him to the incredible world of video games. He still takes his fighting games seriously, but RPGs are his true passion. The Witcher, Persona, Dragon Quest, Mass Effect, Final Fantasy, Trails, Tales — he's played 'em all. A little too much, some might say.
