All these years later, I still don't see the appeal of any Bethesda game. The writing is awful, the dungeons are all boring, character builds are lame plus restrictive, the dungeons are unrewarding and largely copy and pasted, the combat is awful, the story is linear with zero role playing choices and the so called "sandbox elements" amount to going on a killing spree...that's it. You can't interact with the world apart from stealing stuff. You can't climb mountains, cut down trees, use the environment or build anything and there's no environmental destruction.

And the thing is, this is every Bethesda game including the recent Starfield. They're all outdated experiences on release. Anyone expecting Elder Scrolls 6 to be any different or an actual good open world game like Zelda BOTW/TOTK or Crimson Desert is fooling themselves. It won't even have a faction of the mechanics of those games or do them well.

I played it so much on my Xbox 360 that the disc cracked.

One of the worst games I have ever quit. The story is garbage. The mechanics were awful. Just lazy. Even modders had to spend a decade to try to make it playable.

One of the all time greats. I most recently did another full play thorough on PSVR 1 and it was one of the most immersive experiences I’ve had in gaming. Felt like the difference between watching a movie and actually being there. It’s a bit janky round the edges - it always was, but it’s more apparent now in 2026 - but still a stone cold classic.

It never really was the best open world RPG. It was easily one of the most popular. Remembering back to 2011 on ps3 every time my characters head dipped below water my entire ps3 would crash. Not exactly best open world RPG.

Bethesda's influence on gaming cannot be understated. That said, rotting corpses are infested with fewer bugs than a Bethesda game. If only they could figure out how to produce games whose technical stability is equal to their world building, there would be world peace, cancer would be cured, and Jesus Christ himself would probably return.

A question of perspective. Like dozens of other classic games, unless you were there? It's impossible to convey what it was and the impact it had. If you fired up a GameCube and played the original Resident Evil 4? It would feel unplayable, but it's one of the greatest games I've ever played. Same for Metal Gear Solid, or a dozen others. Skyrim was awesome 15 years ago. It is less awesome if you played the Witcher 3, or a few other games it influenced. Red Dead Redemption 2 makes Skyrim look pretty bad, but you can bet every creative mind at Rockstar played Skyrim. It was both a buggy, janky mess and a great, and astonishingly influential, landmark game.

For me personally, Morrowind is more of an all time classic, Skyrim is probably a more complete open world but doesn't have that magical atmosphere of Morrowind that engraved itself in my memory so strongly. Skyrim was great, Morrowind was special. Still, Skyrim was a great game which is quite dated for today standards and gave way to games like Witcher, Cyberpunk 2077 and Kingdom Come. In any case, this is my favourite gaming formula so I'm obsessed with all of these games

Skyrim is still the best game of its genre.

Yeah, yeah, the Witcher 3 (and Witcher 2, which honestly deserves to be brought up far more than it is) has a better main quest and more complete side quests, but the Witcher games are third person RPGs, which does make a bit of a difference in feel. Also, you’re playing as Geralt very clearly, whereas Skyrim, it’s a game where you have so much personal decision as to who the character is.

Yes, Elden Ring, BotW/Totk, and Red Dead 2 have all improved on the immersive open world, but, again, Skyrim is a first person game and you’ve got far more agency in character creation.

Yes, you could argue that Baldur’s Gate 3 has more agency in creation, but, again, there’s something to be said about the first person perspective.

And, with Cyberpunk, you’re playing as V, not as your own very personal character. And honestly, I know there’s a lot of love out there for Cyberpunk, but I cannot divorce my experience of it from its launch status, which was more a comedy than a tragedy of sorts, but it’s not a game I have the love for that others have.

Do Oblivion and Morrowind have better main quests? Oh, absolutely. Fallout 3 and New Vegas may hold that honor as well. And, yet… there’s still something just a little bit more immersive about Skyrim. Fallout 4 didn’t quite replicate it and neither did Starfield.

What it is is the storysensing. Skyrim is the absolute master of this craft. Storytelling is a far more familiar concept, where you’re interpreting a story that you’re meant to experience, but storysensing is the concept of absorbing enough details in a game’s world that you personally tell yourself your character’s story. You subconsciously fill things in and create things mentally in the game that don’t exist, but mesh into the world. You become a character wholly of your own existence as you play and you experience quests as that imagined being would experience them. You choose good or evil. You choose to fulfill your destiny as Dragonborn or not. You choice the guilds you work with, to become a werewolf, a vampire, etc. And it holds up remarkably well today too. And even just a moment back in its world is strangely still as inviting and absorbing as it was all those years ago now. And let me also say that the game has an immense pull with all people, not just those of us that are dedicated gamers. Skyrim was the first game that my wife ever really loved and is likely the only game she will ever hit 100+ hours in. I’ll be honest and say it’s probably my only and last 1000+ hour game. My son is now able to sink into the game and appreciate its majesty and it’s not so complex a game, as many of the other games I’ve listed, that he is repelled from the game pretension. The game understands that it’s a game for everyone. It’s a classic, an all-timer, and it was obvious 15 years ago and it still is today.

Skyrim’s one of the greatest games of all time. Certainly in my personal top 10 list of games of all time. It does have its flaws, but they’re strangely something easy to overlook. I do find the main quest to have quite a weak third act, but yet I’ve been compelled to complete it more times than games with far “better” storylines. And perhaps time had been kind enough to give us some absolutely essential DLCs that do provide deeper storytelling that present epilogues just as immersive as base game. Skyrim is, basically, to video games what the Beatles were to rock music. You can argue why you think it’s overrated, but at the end of the day, it delivers so many hits and everything is so memorable, even though you can see its influences. Todd Howard was right back then when he said, “It just works.” It may have been buggy at times, but he was certainly right.

Skyrim’s so good my post was too long and I didn’t want to edit. 😅

Finished it back in the day, it was great then but tried it about 10 years later and it didn't age well at all.I don't have the nostalgia others do about it, so, for me, there are far better RPG's to play these days.

I still boot Skyrim up once every couple of years. I do quite like the Bethesda style RPG. But also that space has kinda moved on. And both the Kingdom Come games and what CD Projekt are up to are leagues ahead of what Bethesda is doing.

Skyrim is like The Maltese Falcon. It is simply a classic, but there will always be people that say "but it's black and white and theres no special effects etc etc". Thankfully despite the naysayers, there will always be those of us that stood on the balcony on Dragonsreach and just stared in awe into the distance. I've just checked and I've spent 500 hours on the PS4 and PS5 versions alone - god knows how much time I spent on the PS3! It was an incredible achievement despite the flaws and will be talked about long after other games have been forgotten.

That said, I think Oblivon was even better!

My Skyrim experience was on PS3. I went to a midnight launch for it on 11/11/11 (remember those?).

As a huge Morrowind fan, my actual experience playing the game was middling to horrendous though due to game-breaking technical issues (a memory bleed issue in the save file) which rendered my save unplayable. As far as I know, this issue still exists on the PS3.

I never touched the game again, never had a desire to go back. I didn't really like much it did compared to Morrowind, but it was a step up from Oblivion at least. I'd honestly throw it in a 7/10, super forgettable experience - where Morrowind was a solid 10/10 for me.

I think I put ~40-50 hours into it. Beat the story. The most damning thing about the game is I hardly recall much from the experience except same-y side dungeons, constellations in the skill system screen, and a mountain in the middle of the world map. Almost a complete blank.

While I remember every square inch of Morrowind, which I played 20 years ago. I think that says it all and more.

great game to get lost in but I 100% think it needs an upgrade for newer consoles - i'd pay for an upgraded version as long as I could keep my saves - spent tooooo long in the game to lose them

I enjoyed reading your comment. I couldn't help but think while reading though, the ultimate "storysensing" RPG (great term, BTW - totally stealing that) is Morrowind. And Skyrim by that yardstick was a cheap imitation which took what made the earlier games really special and downgraded it.

The scale of that proposition, to do or be anyone you want, is overwhelming in the Elder Scrolls games. And I agree while there are other RPGs which are miles and miles better than any Elder Scrolls game, no other game does this specific element quite as well as the Elder Scrolls. As you mentioned, maybe the first person perspective? Is it the curious lack of real direction (hello Morrowind) which invites you to just explore and find what's out there? The sort of mystique of it all.

Whatever that feeling of possibilities and exploration you are describing, it was not done quite as well in Skyrim as it had been done in Morrowind. For about, 30 different reasons. But I can't help but agree with the overall sentiment anyways these games do (or used to do) something really special.

As you said, Skyrim was a game with more mass market appeal than its predecessors. More accessible, more friendly. And that's awesome. But part of what made Morrowind frankly magical for me was how inaccessible it was - the veil of secrecy over the story, how to progress, and even some of the mechanics themselves. While this initially created a barrier to play, it eventually ramped up the immersion to the ceiling. That enhanced the "storysense" in a very masochistic way which will never be replicated as games become more homogonized and streamlined.

Absolutely still one of the best. Started playing through it again a couple weeks ago and it's still so good even with a vanilla play through.

I've started Skyrim many times, but probably finished the main quest only twice. In comparison I've finished Witcher 3 three times this year. I think my tastes have changed. I used to like the Skyrim sandbox, but I find now I prefer the emotional engagement I have with stories and characters. So for me Skyrim now feels dated.

it is definitely one of the best, same as fallout. Gambits system was absolutely wild.But it depends, original Baldurs Gate, Icewind Dale etc during the launch was someting else. Arcana, Lands of Lore, Ishar, Dungeon Master etc or even amazing Realms of the Haunting, even that one is more fps than rpgif you play some of these today for the first time, its not the same, but if you played it then... different story, different memories

@UnlimitedSevens I totally understand the point of view that Morrowind could be the best Elder Scrolls game, but it lacks a key feature to beat Skyrim and that’s accessibility. As old as Skyrim is, its visuals still stand up fairly well too, which helps. Morrowind, if remastered, I think, would blow some minds, but even so, I think Skyrim would hold the edge for being just so darn inviting as a game. I’ve seen people say, “I had to play Skyrim, even though I’d never played many video games,” which is quite a wonderful thing.

The only thing that matters in gaming is sales numbers so it's a good game based on that alone.

It was a zeitgeist thing. The game is broken, as is the story, but there's a timeless charm to all of its quirks. There's just nothing like Skyrim, and in many departments, it's still head and shoulders over most modern RPGs.

I’ve got the platinum thrice over. The PSVR version was my favorite.

It never was the best of anything. If anything, it's one of the worst. Like literally any Bethesda game. Wtf do you even mean. What is good about Skyrim or any Bethesda game? Literally name just one thing. Not the gameplay, not the graphics, not the dialogue, not the animations, not the details, not the breathing world, not the characters.

@GirlVersusGame It's a mixed bag, haha. The general orientation of the map is similar to Boston and Massachusetts in general (Salem being further north and east, for example). Skyrim somewhere around 1000 hours. Oblivion Remaster around 400 hours. Now waiting for Sentinel and another 1000 hours.

When you find and earn one of the many MW4 DMZ keys, here's where you need to go to use it

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Whether you've earned one of the various MW4 DMZ keys by completing a Story Mission, finding it somewhere on the map, or, dare I say, by killing another player (shame on you), then you might be wondering where to use it.In MW4's DMZ mode, there are loads of keys that unlock valuable lockers and vaults, but their description only gets you to a general area - not the precise location of the wares. To help you out, here's a full list of every DMZ key and where to use it, so if you're looking something in particular, find it with CTRL+F or your browser's search function.

These are all the keys that can be used in the Political Prison area of the map:

Some of the keys can be used at different locations, including the likes of Blackmarket Weapons Lockers and Silo Control Rooms, both of which you can find in this northwest part of the map. This is a common spawn area, as well, so if you have one of these multi-use keys, this is a good place to use it.

Keys 5 to 11 in this list are a little harder to use as you'll need to breach the actual prison, and you'll of course encounter plenty of hostility as you do so.

These are all the DMZ keys that can be used in the Cheongun Village and Mirae Hospital areas of the map:

The village is a fairly simple area to loot as it's lots of small buildings rather than one well-locked down area like the hospital or the casino. The casino is a particularly tough location to get into, so make sure you're well kitted out with your best MW4 guns and a medkit or two.

Speaking of the Casino, the Counting Room Vault key is one of the better keys you'll get early on if you're completing Story Missions, and we've got a handy guide to getting into the DMZ Counting Room Vault if you'd like some help.

Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week

These are the keys that can be used in the Hanuel Nuclear Reactor area of the map:

The Nuclear Reactor area is the hardest location to enter as you'll be faced with a radiation field that will quickly deal you damage if you're not wearing a gas mask. You're still not immune even with a gas mask, though, as they deteriorate in time, so plan your entry into this area carefully, and keep any keys safely in your stash until you're fully ready for the challenge.

These are the keys that can be used in the Songdo Wharf and The Grid areas of the map:

This area is a good place to use any DMZ bank vault keys, as explained in more detail in our standalone guide, as there are three different banks here you can attempt to access (including the one slightly further south, as you'll see below). One is the main bank tower located inside The Grid, though, which itself is a high-threat area, so enter at your own risk.

The following keys are used in the Wolves Stadium and Hajin River Heights areas of the map:

As I've mentioned above, you've got a bank vault on the boundary between this area and The Grid above it, plus another one to the south of the stadium, both of which are pretty easy to access with the right materials. Meanwhile, another of the DMZ police stations is located here, so if you've got both keys and a big enough backpack, it's a great place to hit.

These are the keys that you can use in the Imjin Farmland area of the map:

There isn't much need to come to this area unless you have any of the specific keys above as it's quite an isolated area with not much else going on. Other than the Fire Station Storage key, though, these are all unique to this area, so if you find any, you might want to collect them and hit the area in one go. You may even find some others while you're looking around, so dedicate your entire match to this zone and have a good search.

These are all the keys that are used in the Air Base and Deadtown areas of the map:

This western area of the map is another common spawn area, so if you've got a Blackmarket Locker key or Silo Control Room key, this is a good place to consider. There are also plenty of good weapons to grab around here, so take your time and explore carefully.

#4068. The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel teaser all but confirms Hammerfell setting and means we can finally stop using that eight year old header image with the hills

Say hello to sandy scroll screengrab for the foreseeable future

Praise Talos and whatever other Elder Scrolls deities you might worship. We here at RPS and in the wider gaming press finally have new material to use when hunting for images to symbolise The Elder Scrolls 6. No more will we be limited to that shot of some hills from the 2018 teaser, because Bethesda have shown off an elder scroll covered in sand while revealing the new game's subtitle and all but locking in a setting. As a recent report from The Verge claimed, it's called The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel and looks to be set in Hammerfell.

These details were revealed in a short teaser at the end of a Todd Howard-fronted video celebrating Bethesda Game Studios' 40th anniversary. As such, the majority of the video is the Toddinator recapping the studio's history by touching on each of the games they've put out since 1986's Gridiron. Then, he looks to the future. "You know, everybody’s always asking about Elder Scrolls 6," the Toddfather said. "And we thought, hey, given the moment, what a perfect time to tell you what The Elder Scrolls 6 is actually called."

Cue a shot of an elder scroll buried in sand, followed by the The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel in fancy logo font. Then, a quote attributed to a moth priest called Yazar. "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate." OOH, CRYPTIC. In all seriousness, between the subtitle, the sand, and Yazar being referred to as a moth priest in service of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell, the Verge report's assertion that the game will be set in Hammerfell is essentially set in stone by this teaser even if his Toddliness didn't spell it out himself.

Sentinel's the name of both a kingdom and city in the Redguards' province. The inclusion of an elder scroll in the teaser and the quote from Yazar also lend credence to the Verge report's claim that the game will make a big thing out of unravelling secrets linked to the provenance of these mysterious bits of paper. As for the quote's yammering of lost futures and undone victories, I'll venture to speculate that it could turn out to be reference to the player character thwarting a Thalmor victory, since Skyrim seemed to set up the elves as being on the verge of conquering Tamriel as the Cyrodillic empire fractured and fell.

That may or may not be the case, but we do know for sure that this teaser likely means a huge downturn in use of the header image below. It's eight years old, pulled from The Elder Scrolls 6's infamous 2018 teaser. All these years on, the game's finally on the way. You've served us well, screengrab of some hills. Talos guide you to wherever less regularly used images go.

Elder Scrolls teasing aside, it's worth bearing in mind that Bethesda parent company Microsoft have spent the majority of this year gutting their workforce with mass layoffs and studio ditching. Microsoft are also still currently subject to a BDS movement boycott over their reported ties to the Israeli military.

#4067. Mobile Suit Gundam Battle Operation 3 has been announced, marking another attempt at a free-to-play team game after Gundam Evolution's unfortunate fate

Bandai Namco have released the initial announcement trailer for Mobile Suit Gundam Battle Operation 3, a free-to-play team action game and a sequel to 2018's Battle Operation 2. The trailer is very, very pretty, showing off Gundam units clashing in large-scale battles and infantry fighting beneath the colossal mechas' feet (kinda like Titanfall, in having both human and mecha players in the same match). I'm sadly not yet enough of a true Gundam fan to recognise many of these units on sight other than the RX-78-2, but there's a real variety shown off here.

MOBILE SUIT GUNDAM GUNDAM BATTLE OPERATION 3　Announcement Trailer Watch on YouTube

While there's no release date specified in the trailer, Bandai Namco have confirmed that there will be a network test in Japan through November 20th-22nd, with an open network test planned for the future (thanks, Gematsu).

Following the fate of Gundam Evolution, a 2022 attempt at a hero shooter featuring Gundam units, it's nice to see another shot at taking the Gundam series into a team format. Evolution suffered from the all-too-common trappings of heavy microtransaction inclusion, with several playable Gundam units with unique abilities only available through paying real cash. It was rightly criticised for this, and since Bandai Namco seemed to have had high hopes for the revenue it could make from said microtransactions, the lack of money made meant it shut down just a year later.

Contrastingly, from what I can see, Gundam Battle Operation 2 was received fairly well on its release. While little is actually known about the third game at this point, let's hope it has a better chance than the series' last big release. I will quickly note that the trailer does close with a "*Some content may require purchase" note, so it'll likely have some form of microtransaction in itself — hopefully not to the same degree as Evolution. And, while we're on the topic of Gundam, there's also 2027's Gundam Rogue Orbit, a drastically different game that seems closer to a Devil May Cry-esque action title (though, unlike Battle Operation 3, will begin life as a timed exclusive to PS5). Now, if we could get a Gundam game that plays something like Armored Core, and god willing a proper PC release, I would be a very happy girl.

Original Story: It's Thursday, which means it's time for your latest batch of Xbox Free Play Days titles!

So far, we know of four games in the lineup, thanks to some digging from Redditor Oliomono. Their findings usually match up with the official lineup, but there's a decent chance Xbox will add another one or two games later today to shape up the final list.

We've seen STUFFED and Sunderfolk in the FPD lineup before, so it'll be a little bit pants if this is the bulk of it. The latter title has this interesting gimmick which requires the use of smartphones in order to play. It would be good to see at least two bigger titles added, but at the end of the day, it's just nice that they're free to try over the weekend if you fancy.

Here's what we know about Xbox's latest Free Play Days lineup so far:

You'll require some sort of Xbox Game Pass subscription in order to play all four of these games.

These games should be free to play until late on November 15, with a slight chance to go on longer. It's also par of the course to see discounts attached to FPD games, which makes adding them to your permanent collection a little easier on the wallet.

#4065. Venom-toothed Noxious Terminids are soon to infest Helldivers 2, and it's your noble job to sterilise the galaxy for Super Earth

Helldivers 2 isn't slowing down any time soon, and according to Edwin's recent interview with Arrowhead CCO Johan Pilestedt, it'll continue to be Arrowhead's main priority for the future. As if Helldivers 2 wasn't full of enough horrors for our brave Super Earth Helldivers to shoot at for the betterment of galactic democracy, its next update is due to add an entirely new Terminid subspecies, the Noxious Terminids.

First up on are the Noxious Scavengers. These horrible little (see: huge) things skitter around at high speed and are loaded with deadly poison, but are thankfully at least fragile. Liberal use of area-of-effect weapons such as flamethrowers, explosives and flamethrowers are recommended to avoid being overrun by these horse-sized insects. Then there's the Noxious Spewer, which is not only fast like its smaller brethren despite its larger size, but also equipped with a web projectile which locks a Helldiver in place, vulnerable to a fatal bite. Oh, and if you dare shoot its soft underbelly, it violently explodes, with the same web fluid covering a wide area around it. The poison inflicted by these creatures' bites is a new damage over time effect that can blur vision, slow movement, eat away at your health, and make you fear this may be the end for you — so it's a bit like getting the flu (get your jabs!)

HELLDIVERS™ 2 | A Cleaner Galaxy Starts With You Watch on YouTube

This update also makes the change that bug caves can be found across many more worlds across the galaxy, leading troopers down tunnels with limited visibility and claustrophobic dead ends. Super Earth's propaganda, sorry, I mean, guidance, describes the galactic sterilisation program quite simply: locate the invasive species, identify the horrific monsters at the barrel of your flamethrower, and sterilise (burn to cinders). The guidance also, hilariously, includes the line: "Super Earth reminds you that ammunition is cheaper than antivenom." Now, get out there and rid our beautiful democracy of this vile pestilence.

#4064. Frostpunk 2's The Surge DLC keeps the wintery apocalypse and adds in faction-clash-inducing electricity and sets a seasonally appropriate December release date

For the time being, the world of Frostpunk remains a hypothetical, even if it's one that seems just that little bit more likely than I'd like it to be given who's in charge of the world. But at the very least, there are pockets of hope to be found in Frostpunk 2, namely with its newly revealed next bit of DLC, The Surge, a name that has been bequeathed to it for incredibly obvious reasons. Oh, you need me to explain them? Fiiiiine.

You and your probably not so merry band of survivors have been trekking across the UK, when you end up at a "mysterious valley." Apparently some rumours have been going round about a "marvel left behind by history’s greatest mind - a relic with the potential to reshape the world itself." So you go off to look for it, and it essentially seems like this relic lets you use a whole bunch of electricity. Only, despite how useful this is for automating a bunch of work, various factions disagree over how it should be used, "while the secrets hidden within the valley prove far more difficult to uncover than anyone expected."

In terms of what you should expect from this DLC, for starters there's a new scenario to check out "set in an entirely new region, far beyond the borders explored in Frostpunk 2 so far." This relic is also implied to have come from the mind of one Nikola Tesla, you know, the electricity guy. There'll apparently be ways to utilise the Great Storm that's ruined the planet to "turn catastrophic whiteouts into valuable, harvested and stored resources." And you'll have some hidden treasures to find and mysterious to uncover in various nearby caves and ruins.

All sounds neat enough! And it's not too far away either. The Surge is currently slated for a seasonally appropriate December 14th release date. Let's hope no real world environmental disasters get in the way of that, 'ey? While you wait for it, you can wishlist the DLC on Steam.

This might be the best chassis of 2026. It doesn't tick all the boxes perfectly, but what it does do at this price is deliver an exceptionally good looking case, with plenty of cable management, and a primo build experience that puts even some of the bigger case manufacturers to shame. Available in both black and white, for those looking for a modest rig that'll look good on your desk, the C6 Curve is it.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

Shangri-la, the promised land. Aside from the very notion of that concept being oh so appetising in the chaotic world that is 2026, there's something of that in the C6 Curve Air. An odd way to start a chassis review, I'll admit, particularly one that genuinely, I think is probably one of the best PC cases of 2026, but it's more than a metaphor here.

This feels like something a little special this case. It feels like how Corsair's 4000D series felt, or NZXT's H7 lineup when that first debuted, or even Phanteks' Evolv arsenal from way back when at the start of my tech journalism career. There's something iconic here, that I can't quite place my finger on, something that I think is massively underrated in the world of custom rigs. Refined subtlety.

Honestly the C6 Curve Air feels as if it's some bastard love child of the Phanteks Evolv series, Asus's Pro Art line and Fractal Design's North variants. Born in secret, and somehow less than $100.

It's clean, modest, with an elegant aesthetic, good choice of materials, dependable internal layout, decent cable management, and it's genuinely a chassis that I can't stop looking at. It's not flawless, nothing ever is, but what Antec has done here is, particularly in a market that's so over saturated with tempered glass black obelisks, is impressive.

✅ You want a budget, clean chassis that stands out from the crowd: With curved tempered glass, a stylish base, and a remarkably crisp interior at an outstanding price point the C6 Curve Air, is one of the best looking affordable cases you can find on the market today.

✅ You're using a massive graphics card: Bells and whistles are minimal in the C6 Curve Air to save on cost of manufacturing, which means there's no anti-sag bracket included. If you're using a larger triple-slot, pick up an aftermarket anti-sag mount elsewhere.

1x USB 3.2 Type-C, 2x USB 3.2 Type-A, 3.5 mm headphone jack

2x 120 mm PSU SHROUD; 3x 120 mm/2x140 mm ROOF; 1x 120/140 mm REAR

ATX (160 mm side-mounted, 150mm traditional)

At a surface level, there's not a huge amount to talk about here in terms of overall featureset. It's a typical mid-tower case, it's got support for ATX, there's some nice rubber grommets built in to hide the cables protruding from the rear, it's got a full PSU shroud, and some fairly modest fan and rad mounting locations dotted around the place, and well that's about it. The big standout feature is of course, the tempered glass. It's curved along the front edges, and wraps around midway back through the rear of the chassis, but there's no special innovative, screaming from the rooftops technical element at play here.

That glass is a curious decision as well, because it cuts your case cable management space down in half, and there's no additional intake mounting points either, nor front nor side, other than the two (included) 120 mm fans situated in the floor itself.

But here's the thing with the C6 Curve Air. These small seemingly mundane features that it has, that we've seen in cases for the last ten years, are so well refined, that it's almost like a complete fresh launch.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

Take the intake fans. They're twin 120 mm reverse blade designs, recessed into the floor of the PSU shroud. Now, that's a space usually taken up by a hard drive caddy (which very few of us use), and an abundance of excess stuffed cables. To counter that, Antec's opted for no caddy there at all, leaving one mounting location on the back of the CPU tray, and redesigned the entire PSU area, so it's rotational by its nature.

You can slot a 160 mm PSU in here, sideways, with a power lead passthrough, and route all the cables directly up the back of the motherboard tray. No need for a Corsair RMx Shift here, no sir, any old PSU will do. That means, cable management routes are remarkably direct, and there's little mess to manage or tight corners to wrap your cables around.

As for the actual cable management, there's not a mad amount of support here either. There's a few velcro straps, and three plastic clips on the right, and those rubber grommets and that's it, but it's enough, and if you tuck your extra SATA cables out of the way, those twin 120 mm intakes have plenty of space to pull air up and through. It's actually one of the cleanest cable managed cases I've built, and there's not a single tie in sight.

Both sides, and the entire base of the chassis are well ventilated as well, with either that pristine slat design lining the front and edges, or pure perforations, so cool airflow is ample. It's all just very well thought out.

The only thing that mildly irked me, was a lack of a removable radiator bracket, (which would've made subsequent cable management at the end considerably easier), and there's no GPU anti-sag bracket either, which has almost become a staple in modern designs.

And that's all coming in at just around the $100 mark, if not cheaper. Antec, also has a white variant available too, for a little extra if you do fancy something a bit punchier in terms of the overall aesthetic.

There are alternatives out there, that allow you to fit more kit in, mount more fans etc, but few cases feel quite as good as what you're getting here. Hyte's Y40 is a good example, or Lian Li's O11 Vision Compact.

And of course you can get some flashier cases as well, Phanteks' XT View Matrix with its full dot grid display, again fits in that groove. But none of them feel particularly timeless compared to this.

There is one caveat to all of this of course, and that's long term future viability here. Although the case design itself will last for many years to come, let's say hypothetically RAM and silicon manufacturing ramp up by 300% in the next two years somehow, and datacenter demand drops (we can only hope), and you do want to build a new machine with new more power hungry hardware, I do have some concern that those twin 120 mm intakes, might not be quite enough to cool both a thirsty GPU and CPU combo longer into the future.

I've waxed lyrically about how this thing looks visually already, but it's worth stressing because it's a thing of beauty. There is absolutely something "ProArty" about the C6 Curve Air. Even if it's just its design philosophy. The slats, the power button, the understated lack of lighting, the curved glass. It's undeniably luscious in scope. Heck even that roof panel, slimline, compact, smooth against the top just sings to the overall design, and that blend of perforated mesh around the PSU area, sits strikingly against the slats feeding the intake fans, and it really stands out.

It's overall a little wider than you'd think for a mid-tower, particularly given the height (in part to accommodate the rotated PSU), but given we've got so many cuboid styled dual chamber cases these days, I'm not opposed to a little extra girth (don't quote me on that).

Perhaps, and this is very debatable, but perhaps it's just slightly too understated? A touch of integrated LED lighting, just a soft warm white glow somewhere, shining up inside the interior, and illuminating your hardware, following the old adage, show the light, not the lightbulb, would work a treat in this thing. It's the first aftermarket addition I'd look at adding that's for sure, as it'd just give it a bit more depth inside.

As for building in the C6 Curve Air, it's a fairly smooth ride. The first major hurdle I came across was actually dismantling the chassis. I tend not to look at instruction manuals on a new case, because in my mind, it should be intuitive. There's only so many ways you can attach things to a black box afterall.

The glass side panel pops off and out from the rear, and then slides up. The rear metal panel does the same, as does the secondary rear glass panel too. You pull up from the rear of the roof panel to grab the underside there, and then you're left with that front curved glass, and the two PSU shroud covers. For the PSU covers, simply pull them up from the bottom, and as for the front, I for the life of me couldn't figure out how to remove it. You can remove two philips screws, and then tilt it out away from the main spine, but it doesn't seem to come up and out like the others, at least not easily. That is fine really, as you can leave that on anyway. There's no fans to mount here, and it acts as a brace for the whole structure.

Other things to note, there is of course that passthrough PSU plate on the back. You can remove that if you're running a short 150 mm PSU, but if you're using a 160 mm you'll need to rotate the unit, and then hook it up to the passthrough. Antec's included a cutout to thread the passthrough cable through as well, although it will depend on the positioning of the port on your power supply. Remember to keep the PSU with the fan facing down, as the shroud is solid above it.

Cable management on the whole was surprisingly impressive. There's not a ton that you can do here. Antec has included two velcro straps to help manage the 24-pin and front I/O cables, and then there's some plastic clips on the right (designed for fans, but I stuck EPS power in here as well), and that's it, but surprisingly, combined with the rubber grommets, it was enough. I used a total of one cable tie in this entire build, and to be fair, I'd already pre-strapped that to the 12VHPWR cable anyway prior to this system.

The only downsides during my time with the C6 Curve Air came in the form of the lack of a radiator bracket, (which meant I ended up fiddling for far too long trying to plug in the pump), and there's no GPU anti sag solution anywhere. Although to be fair, I'm not exactly sure where you'd fit one in this design.

So, it's a good case, we've established that, but is there anything we can do during the build process to make it better? Well if it was my own rig, I'd be looking at shifting the fan layout, away from a traditional setup. Keep the two 120 mm floor intakes as is (maybe shift them out to something with a bit more pushing power), but then I'd also swap the 360 mm AIO exhausts to act as intakes instead. A ballsy move, working against thermodynamics, I get it, but I'd absolutely test whether overall you'd see better temps long-term with that config. That way you've got a five in, one out solution, for massive positive pressure, in exchange for slightly higher CPU temps.

On the cable management front, keep your cabling as minimal as possible, remove any you don't need, but even if you leave them in, it's not the end of the world, and lastly I'd leave installing the radiator, until the very end (before the GPU), once all the cables had been plugged in (including the pump and CPU fans), just to make life a little easier.

Oh and 100% install the PSU rotated, rather than removing that rear bracket. It just gives you so much more space, and I can't stress enough, just how easy it is routing those cable runs as a result.

4. Best budget compact: Thermaltake S100 TG Snow Edition

This might be the best chassis of 2026. It doesn't tick all the boxes perfectly, but what it does do at this price is deliver an exceptionally good looking case, with plenty of cable management, and a primo build experience that puts even some of the bigger case manufacturers to shame. Available in both black and white, for those looking for a modest rig that'll look good on your desk, the C6 Curve is it.

After graduating from the University of Derby in 2014, Zak joined the PC Format and Maximum PC team as its resident staff writer. Specializing in PC building, and all forms of hardware and componentry, he soon worked his way up to editor-in-chief, leading the publication through the covid dark times. Since then, he’s dabbled in PR, working for Corsair for a while as its UK PR specialist, before returning to the fold as a tech journalist once again.

He now operates as a freelance tech editor, writing for all manner of publications, including PC Gamer, Maximum PC, Techradar, Gamesradar, PCGamesN, and Trusted Reviews as well. If there’s something happening in the tech industry it’s highly likely Zak has a strong opinion on it.

#4062. Xbox Anniversary Weapon Skins For Gears Of War: E-Day Are Now Free To Claim

Celebrate Xbox's 25 years by chainsawing Locust grubs

Xbox's 25th anniversary is just around the corner, and to celebrate the massive milestone, The Coalition is giving away a free translucent green weapon skin bundle in Gears of War: E-Day.

If I'm being honest, it's not massive news, but it's a nice freebie for E-Day players. We're feeling a little merry for Xbox's anniversary on Sunday, so why not? Here's a look at all 12 weapons with the 'Xbox Anniversary' skin pack equipped.

The skin looks lovely across all weapons, but I'm particularly fond of how it looks on the Ripper and Longshot. If you'd like to claim the bundle for yourself, simply boot Gears: E-Day, head to the Store and claim it for free.

Gears joins Halo: Campaign Evolved and Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 in celebrating the quarter-century milestone with a translucent green skin. My favourite has gotta be that Xbox M4 skin in MW4, but seeing as this is an E-Day freebie, you best believe I'll be rocking the Xbox Anniversary bundle in Versus.

In fact, Xbox recently announced a last-minute restock of Xbox Series X25 consoles on the Microsoft Store. Meanwhile, Gears of War: E-Day Season 2: Legacy begins December 1st, bringing with it a whole host of fan-favourite maps, character skins, and more.

#4061. Resident Evil Requiem Wins the First 2026 Game of the Year Award

Top accolade at the Golden Joystick Awards

Resident Evil Requiem has been crowned the Ultimate Game of the Year at the Golden Joystick Awards, the first major games award ceremony of 2026.

Alongside the biggest award, it was also named the Console Game of the Year, and it won categories celebrating the best lead performer (Angela Sant'Albano as Grace Ashcroft) and the best game trailer. Most of the Golden Joystick Awards are decided by a public vote, and the race for Ultimate Game of the Year was extremely close.

Resident Evil Requiem won the award with 17% of the overall vote, but Phantom Blade Zero was right behind it with 16% and then Crimson Desert got 15%.

Obviously, since it's not out yet, GTA 6 wasn't eligible for any categories.

Elsewhere, the award for the Best Remake / Remaster went to The Witcher 3 Remastered, then Dispatch won the Best Soundtrack and Best Storytelling categories. Onimusha: Way of the Sword has the Best Audio Design according to the voters, Valheim was the year's Best Indie Game, and The Witcher 4 is the Most Wanted Game.

Do you agree with the winners at the Golden Joystick Awards? Share your reaction in the comments below.

#4060. Play as water and rain on wildfires in Atuel, a short, free game about the power and vulnerability of nature

Well, have you played Atuel? If not, you can do so within the next hour - it's a tiny, free, 25-minute walking sim, albeit one with little actual walking on account of you playing most of it as a river. More of a running sim, really.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

Technically, Atuel calls itself a "documentary game", and not without justification. While its sweeping Patagonian landscapes are rendered with a dreamy otherworldliness, and certain moments are downright mystic, the whole watery journey is based directly on the Atuel River that runs through western Argentina. As you drift downhill, taking control of water, clouds, and the local wildlife, you'll hear real-life scientists and historians monologuing on the Atuel and its relationship with the human cultures it's nourished. Mercifully, these are delivered with thoughtfulness as well as earnestness, maintaining the game's contemplative atmosphere without making it sound like the audio guide to a museum of Birmingham canals.

A few bends in, Atuel also takes on the climate crisis, directing you away from the soothing freshwater and into wildfires and parched riverbeds. I'd say this was preaching to the choir, at least for anyone who a) desires a functioning planet and b) learned about the water cycle in primary school, but then it isn't really preaching. Rather, developers Matajuegos weave between the beauty of the Earth and the need to protect it quite gracefully, and end their river tour on a more hopeful note than its darker moments may have intimated.

There's plenty else to leave an outsized impression in your memory matter: the understated, naturally-textured soundtrack, for instance, or the patiently gradual zoom-outs that slowly unveil the Andes' wild splendour. For me, and without wanting to undermine the importance or the accuracy of Atuel's environmental point, it was mainly just nice – therapeutic, even – to float through its gorgeous, surreal scenery like a cloud. And sometimes, as one. You can download it for free from Steam and Itch, with a pay-what-you-want option on the latter.

#4059. Silica, an FPS and RTS hybrid that mixes a smidge of Dune and Helldivers together, has left early access and entered 1.0

The concept of fusing an RTS and an FPS always sounds like a fun one, and since 2023 Martin Melichárek has been trying to make a new take on the combination under the watchful eye of DayZ devs Bohemia Interactive through Silica. Today marks the day that Silica leaves early access and enters 1.0, fully fleshing out its hybrid and mish mash of Dune's Arrakis and Helldivers' Terminids.

Digging into Silica a touch more deeply, it is a sci-fi shooter set on a planet where there's a fancy resource you're trying to mine that definitely isn't the spice. There are two warring factions competing for said resource, when, uh oh! Some bug-ish, giant aliens aren't very happy you're doing all that. So, you can either join the fray on the ground with some classic first-person shooting alongside your friends, or you can take the role of commander and dictate your artillery from above.

The 1.0 update obviously comes with a few additions, namely the Centauri Campaign, a "story-driven single-player experience set in the war for Baltarus. It opens with a cinematic intro and features fully voiced mission briefings and in-game dialogue. Between missions, a 3D planetary globe tracks the war as territory changes hands." Commanding your army should be a better experience now too, with the ability to "arrange units into formations, issue more precise movement and attack orders, and quickly select all units of the same type. Improved AI targeting and vehicle movement also help your armies operate more effectively in large-scale battles."

Beyond that, 1v1 matchmaking has been added in, where you can fight against another commander. The Steam Workshop sandbox tools have been expanded for building your own scenarios and sharing them with others. And there are a whole bunch of bug fixes, quality-of-life improvements and additions, and more. You can read about some of those in more detail in this handy little blog post. If you like what Silica is putting down, then you can pick it up on Steam.

#4058. The Citadel Project is a Thief-inspired dark fantasy, survival-horror lite stealth-em-up with some lovely shadows set in a medieval megastructure

You know, given the whole stealthy element of Thief-like immersive sims, I'm surprised there haven't been more of them with horror elements. There's Gloomwood, sure, but it's not as common as I'd like. That in turn then makes me curious about The Citadel Project, an immersive sim with some survival-horror elements set in a nasty, parasite-infected dark fantasy world, all apparently made by just one person.

In The Citadel Project, "the last line of defense built by the Ancient Kings in an attempt to preserve what remains of humanity in the face of the Great Storm." Some kind of evil force is ruining it from the inside, and you have to make your way through a medieval megastructure to figure out what happened. You aren't anyone special, "just a simple prisoner who manages to escape from a cell deep within the Citadel." Truthfully, the story sounds fine enough, I'm more smitten with the vibes put on display.

The shadows are what sells me, for the most part. They're dark and moody, looking plenty ripe for hiding in. And look, if you hand me a megastructure to explore, I'm going to do so. I'm also a fan of your main weapon, a crossbow. Not enough games with crossbows if you ask me! There's all sorts of bolts you can use with it, like a fire bolt that, obviously, sets things or enemies alight, a rope bolt to help you quickly climb or swing out of danger, a decoy bolt that makes a lot of sound to distract with, or a moss bolt; I'm not sure what that one does, my guess would be to dampen your footsteps and make it easier to sneak up on unsuspecting baddies.

Said baddies also appear to be infected with some kind of parasite, the severing of which appears to come in handy when trying to take them down. Overall, The Citadel Project likes a neat little im sim with just enough going on to make me curious to explore further. Which I might do, when I get the chance, as there is a demo available on Steam. Alternatively, I could just wait a week, as the game is out in early access November 11th, just over a week away. You can wishlist it on Steam right here.

#4056. "Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop": Salacious Fire Emblem-ish Food Devils gets a delay because its devs think Valve is inundated with genAI games

You might have seen that for today's grub, Edwin decided to in part feed The Maw with Food Devils, an incredibly salacious, foodie take on Fire Emblem, as it was meant to release today. The only problem is, it's not actually out yet. That might prompt you to call Edwin a rotten liar and march up to his castle at the top of the hill on a dark and stormy night with pitchforks and torches, but I beseech you to wait, because it's actually Steam's fault. And potentially, it's the fault of all those awful AI games that have been flooding Steam recently.

In a Steam blog post shared earlier today, developer Studio Daimon explained why the game isn't able to be released today, first offering a bit of context: if you want to put your game on Steam, you have to submit for approval so that it matches what you've described and doesn't harbour malware, amongst other reasons. As the post explains, "before submitting a build, devs see a disclaimer that says 'This review typically takes 3-5 business days, but please allow up to 7 business days in case feedback needs to be addressed'." Except the team submitted their build on October 12th, more than 20 days ago, with no approval in sight.

The reason? "We can only assume it's because Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop, but the whole process is now taking several weeks for some developers." For some context, Game Discovery Tool did some statistics magic and found that more than 50% of games released in October on Steam featured an AI disclosure. Valve have required that games disclose AI use since January 2024, and a year on from then in January 2025 only just over 14% of games featured such a disclosure. In January 2026, that jumped up to a little over 25%, and now here we are at more than 50%.

And to be clear, Steam releases have gone up too. According to SteamDB data, a little over 2000 games were released on the platform in October 2025. But in October 2026, that has jumped up to almost 4000. Correlation is obviously not causation, so take that with a pinch of salt. Still, it paints a concerning image over AI usage, and potentially sounds like it's affecting how Valve operates. Almost as if allowing free reign over AI is bad, or something!

Unfortunately for Studio Daimon, there's no estimate on when Food Devils might launch. "Even now, we don't know when Steam will give us the final OK to finally release our game," they wrote. "We sent another ticket last week saying that the situation was urgent and that we might miss our release date because of this, but it also got ignored. I'm sure that their staff is just too overwhelmed at the moment, but these sudden and massive delays have affected many developers throughout October, with some even being forced to postpone their releases... including us."

They're hoping to still be able to release it by the end of the week, but "can't make any plans or promises because it's out of our control." Perhaps in the meantime, for those who like what's cooking in the devs' kitchen, we could throw the game a wishlist to be ready for whenever it does launch.

#4055. 'You'll Own Nothing': Sony Wins Hall of Shame Award for Deciding to Kill Physical Discs

I can't imagine this is something Hermen Hulst will want to display on his mantelpiece: PlayStation and Sony have won a Hall of Shame award, called a Shonky Award, from an Australian outlet for its decision to stop making physical discs.

Choice, an Australian website, runs an annual Hall of Shame series, known as the Shonky Awards, where it highlights the "worst products and services uncovered by our experts this year". In 2026, PlayStation finds itself with a Shonky Award alongside Virgin Australia, Ticketmaster, and more companies.

This is because of the company's decision to end PlayStation disc production from January 2028, combined with its current EULA (End-User License Agreement) tied to digital game purchases. A lot of the Choice write-up focuses on the latter:

"In this age of instant gratification, it doesn’t get much more convenient than being able to easily download a movie or video game to your collection to start enjoying immediately," it opens with. "But will you be enjoying them for years to come? That’s less certain."

The site then continues: "Because, according to Sony Interactive Entertainment, you don’t actually own the movies and games that you buy as a digital download instead of a disc. Instead, you’re buying a licence to access the content via Sony’s various digital storefronts, such as the PlayStation Store."

News Sony Reminds PS5 Owners Their Digital Games Are Licensed, Not Sold

But Steam, Xbox, and Nintendo all say the same

News No Disc, No Buy and PS5 Blackout Protests Fail to Impact PlayStation

Active users increases, digital sales percentage increases

It speaks about how Sony still "owns your digital media", and how, in reality, you're actually buying a "long-term rental". Choice then points to the sudden removal of Studio Canal movies from the PS Store, where refunds weren't offered.

The decision to stop physical PlayStation discs is then discussed, with worries over digital ownership arising once more. It analyses the EULA once more, but as we've pointed out in the past, the terms of Sony's license agreement are virtually identical to that of Xbox, Nintendo, and PC platform Steam.

All their terms of use speak about how the content you're buying is a license — you don't own it. Allow me to reshare the research editor Sammy Barker put into his previous piece concerning the EULAs on other platforms:

The Content and Services are licensed, not sold. Your license confers no title or ownership in the Content and Services. To make use of the Content and Services, you must have a Steam Account and you may be required to be running the Steam client and maintaining a connection to the Internet.

All Digital Goods are licensed, not sold. Your right to access or use any Digital Good is subject to your compliance with: (a) all license terms, license limitations, codes of conduct, and payment terms in the Terms; (b) your payment in full for the applicable Digital Good; (c) these Rules, and; (d) any additional terms provided when you acquire your license.

Subject to the terms of this Agreement, Nintendo grants you a non-exclusive, revocable license to use the Software solely on the Console for your personal, non-commercial use. For clarity, the Software is licensed, not sold, to you, and you may not make use of the Software except as expressly authorized by this Agreement.

These all read very similarly and mean the exact same thing: on all the major video game platforms, you purchase a license to play a video game; you don't own the actual video game.

However, because Sony is removing the option of buying physical PlayStation discs in just over a year to channel all of its business into the PS Store, it's catching considerably more scrutiny than anyone else.

For that, PlayStation wins a Shonky Award from Choice.

"You can’t protect your licensed media based on the current EULA, and there won’t be any alternatives once the discs go away. You’ll own nothing," it concludes.

[source choice.com.au, via gamesradar.com]

Its always been this way - the terms haven't changed - the ONLY difference is that with Physical discs, that licence is embedded on that bit of plastic and you can sell, trade or let a friend borrow that Licence but with Digital, that licence is locked to your Digital account. Its a bit more tricky to block access to a Physical Licence but that hasn't stopped a number of games being 'unplayable' regardless of whether you bought a licence on disc or digitally - Destiny, Marvels Avengers, Anthem etc all now just coasters or 'landfill trash'.

What you purchase, as you always have, is a licence to access and use the Software belonging to a Publisher/developer on whatever platform you have. Just because you have a Licence to play BF6 on PS5, doesn't mean you can play on PC, Xbox or Steam as they'll sell you a licence to access that software on their Platform too.

Even back when games were supplied on Cartridges, you purchased a licence to play the Software loaded on to those cartridges. They obviously have to supply the software to you in some way so you can access it with your licence, but you don't 'own' the Software and if you tried to copy it and distribute it because you 'think' you own it, that's Piracy and always has been.

Not saying I agree with the way Digital is limiting customers ability to 'sell, trade or share' their Licence in the exact same way they can with Physical Not saying I am 'happy' that big Corporations are being more 'anti-consumer'. In theory, we 'should' own our Licences as we always have and should have the right to sell, trade etc but we've never owned the software and as games/hardware have become more integrated with the internet, its enabled the owners of that software/hardware to block or remove access. The Licence isn't as 'permanent' as it once was. You can still use your licence to play N64 games but many games or content aren't playable today even if you own the Disc because they've turned off the Servers - you can't play Killzone online anymore and like I said, can't play Destiny, Anthem or Marvels Avengers either whether you bought on disc or not.

A "server issue" knocked both games offline, across all platforms, for nearly two weeks.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A little less than two weeks after their multiplayer features were taken offline because of a mysterious "server issue," multiplayer functionality in Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3 has been restored, meaning invasions and messages are once again working as they should.

Word of the service restoration game via a very businesslike message on the Dark Souls website: "Regarding the temporary suspension of the game server for Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3, the investigation has been completed and the fix has been applied. The game server and online features are now restored.

"We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience caused, and thank you for your patience and understanding."

So what exactly went wrong? Well, that's the mysterious part. Aside from intermittent apologies for the inconvenience and thanks for your patience in messages posted to X, FromSoft's had nothing to say about it—and that remains the case now: It's back, be happy, speak of the matter no more.

Whatever happened, it clearly wasn't as serious a problem as the 2022 mess that saw PC servers for all Dark Souls games shut down for the better part of a year. In that case, FromSoft copped to the problem: A security vulnerability that allowed malicious code to be executed via the games' online services. But that fix was also long in coming because FromSoft was busy with other things, like finishing Elden Ring, which was kind of a big deal.

Anyway, aside from the relative brevity of the downtime, we had something else that made the outage a little more bearable than it was back in '22: The Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3 Seamless Co-op mods that operate independently of FromSoft's servers. They also enable a far more flexible multiplayer experience than what's offered by the games themselves, letting players team up to run through the games at will, and without having to deal with disconnects when somebody dies or a boss gets smoked.

But if your preference is for the chaos of native Dark Souls multiplayer? Now that option's back on the table too.

#4053. Ubisoft are reportedly tapped as one potential company that could acquire Arkane, though the Dishonored studio's own management may be in the running too

I'd really like it if it weren't Ubisoft though

Things are potentially looking up for Arkane, depending on how you feel about Ubisoft (and depending on who actually ends up acquiring them). I mention the Assassin's Creed developer because, reportedly, they're interested in buying the studio from Microsoft, having even made a bid for it. I'll go out on a limb here and say it's the whole being French thing, but uh, I'd really rather someone else bought Arkane.

This comes from, you guessed it, Bloomberg, who say that sources they've spoken with claim two other gaming companies have also made a bit. There is even the potential that Arkane would be sold to their own management, as Xbox are considering such a move. But overall, it doesn't yet sound like anything is leaning any particular way, as Xbox haven't formalised a deal with any of the potential buyers. Bloomberg also note that if a deal is made, this should then allow Arkane to finish their work on their Blade game, which is expected to release within the next couple of years.

Apparently an Xbox spokesperson told Bloomberg that the gaming company is exploring their options ahead of their December deadline, but didn't comment any further. Ubisoft reportedly did not have a comment to make on the matter. For some context on that December deadline, because of French labour laws, companies that have over 1000 staff members are required to search for a buyer for three months before they can just completely shut down. That makes December 13th the final date that such a deal has to be made by, meaning there's about a month and a half left to go.

Arkane's sale comes as part of a sweeping range of cuts, sales and closures being made by Microsoft at the moment. In July, it was announced that studios like Double Fine, Undead Labs and Compulsion would no longer be a part of Xbox, with all three going indie; Ninja Theory was also announced as part of these cuts, but unfortunately it's looking like they'll be shutting their doors. Thousands of Xbox staff were also laid off at this time, with more laid off in September, and even more coming this month and January reportedly. As always, solidarity with all workers affected by Microsoft's heartless and money hungry cuts.

#4052. Asha Sharma Issues Statement On Xbox's 25th Anniversary And The Future Of Gaming

"Our largest studios will be able to pursue ambitions as far beyond today’s games"

We've been waiting all week for Xbox to acknowledge its 25th anniversary in a formal fashion, and Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has now issued a statement discussing the past, present and future of the brand to celebrate its birthday.

It's a pretty lengthy statement, and a lot of it is just about recapping the history of Xbox and Microsoft Gaming as a whole. Sharma talks about how things have come a long way since "Microsoft Adventure" in 1979, and then how Xbox was "impossible to miss" in 2001 while also revolutionising online play and being there for the launch of Halo.

There's also a cool high-definition ad for the original Xbox console that you can see down below.

"When the original XBOX launched in 2001, it was impossible to miss. It was 2-3x larger than rival consoles, with a giant X molded into a black enclosure and a bright alien green jewel at the center..."

"A year later, Xbox Live revolutionized online play with persistent friend lists and matchmaking, as well as a common service for developers to build connected experiences. And bringing all of this together was Halo: Combat Evolved, a launch title that not only defined XBOX but proved its first advertising campaign: “Games Will Never Be The Same.”

After going through the history, Sharma mentions that each of the 111 people who have worked at Xbox since the beginning will be getting "a special engraved console to commemorate what you’ve helped build".

She then references the fans, Xbox FanFest and how today's FanFest event in Seattle will "bring the celebration home".

"The story of XBOX has never been ours alone. Our fans have challenged us, cheered us on, held us accountable, and stuck with us. We’ve been celebrating this anniversary with fans around the world and special launches. Today, we are bringing the celebration home to Seattle."

And finally, the most notable bit in this statement is probably what she says about the "next 25" years of Xbox, highlighting that the "cost, resources, and risk required" to create modern games has grown dramatically, and that it's had an impact on the ability to turn ideas into games, or at least allow those ideas to reach their potential.

As a result, she says it's something that "must" be changed, and that people and small teams will "soon" be able to achieve things that currently require much larger teams and financial resources in today's world.

"While modern games demonstrate the heights of human craft in ways unimaginable just decades ago, the cost, resources, and risk required to create them have grown just as dramatically. As a result, too many ideas never become games, and too many games fall short of what their creators imagined. For decades, this has been the unavoidable tradeoff of ambition. We must change this."

"Throughout human history, the scale of what we could create was determined by the people, capital, and resources we could command. That relationship is beginning to break. A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations. A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars. And our largest studios will be able to pursue ambitions as far beyond today’s games as Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 is from its first entry in 1982."

"I believe the future of gaming will look more like its beginning, when a small team with a big idea could change how the world plays. Our responsibility is to deliver great games, unmistakable hardware, and give more people the chance to make something the world has never seen."

There's some interesting stuff in here for sure, and we reckon it might be worth keeping an eye on tonight's Seattle Xbox FanFest event for any potential announcements - after all, it's the final stop and "home" destination for the FanFest tour.

For now though, let us know what you think about Asha Sharma's statement down below!

Yes. The passage is strongly AI-related, although it never explicitly mentions artificial intelligence.

It appears to be alluding to the transformative potential of AI, particularly generative AI, in video game development.

1. "A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations."

2. "A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers."

3. "The cost, resources, and risk required to create them have grown dramatically."

No. The passage deliberately avoids mentioning AI, machine learning, or generative AI.

The underlying message is that AI and emerging technology will fundamentally change the economics and scale of video game development.

The author is suggesting that the next generation of games will be created with fewer people, fewer resources, and significantly greater creative ambition.

The wording is particularly interesting because it frames AI not simply as a way to cut jobs or costs, but as a way to enable creative possibilities that were previously impossible.

My verdict: I would interpret this as an indirect statement about the future of AI in gaming, with AI likely being a major part of the vision, even though the passage carefully avoids naming it directly.
